王之涣.b: High Tang poet of whom only six poems survive — but two of them, on Stork Tower and the Liangzhou frontier, are among the most famous ever written.

孟浩然.b: The great landscape poet of the High Tang who never held office, living as a recluse near Xiangyang. Friend of Li Bai and Wang Wei, whose name is always paired with his ("Wang–Meng").

王翰.b: Wealthy, flamboyant High Tang poet; one wine-soaked frontier quatrain made him immortal.

王昌龄.b: Called "the Lord of the Seven-character Quatrain". Master of frontier poems and of the laments of palace women; twice exiled, killed during the An Lushan rebellion.

李颀.b: High Tang poet of frontier ballads and of music, famed for his portraits of musicians and soldiers.

王维.b: Poet, painter, musician and devout Buddhist — "in his poems there are paintings, in his paintings poems". Master of quiet landscape verse written at his Wangchuan estate. Called the "Poet Buddha".

李白.b: Also Li Po. The "Immortal of Poetry": a free spirit who wandered the empire with sword and wine jug, served briefly at Emperor Xuanzong's court, and wrote with dazzling spontaneity of the moon, mountains, friendship and wine. With Du Fu, the greatest of Chinese poets.

高适.b: Frontier poet who, unusually for a poet, rose to high military command. His verse is bold and generous-hearted.

杜甫.b: The "Sage of Poetry". Lived through the An Lushan rebellion that shattered the Tang, and recorded it — war, famine, refugees, his own poverty — with unmatched compassion and craft. His poems are called "poetic history".

岑参.b: Spent years in the far western garrisons of Central Asia; the greatest painter in words of deserts, snowstorms and the frontier.

卢纶.b: One of the "Ten Talents of the Dali era", known for his crisp frontier songs.

李益.b: Mid-Tang frontier poet whose quatrains were set to music and sung across the empire.

白居易.b: Also Po Chü-i. Believed poems should be understood by everyone — he read drafts to an old woman and rewrote what she could not follow. Author of *The Song of Everlasting Sorrow* and *The Pipa Player*, and of satires on the people's suffering.

杜牧.b: The "Little Du" (to Du Fu's "Old Du"). A brilliant, romantic late Tang poet of Yangzhou nights and southern landscapes, and a sharp critic of history.

李商隐.b: The most mysterious of Chinese poets — his "Untitled" love poems are dense with allusion and longing, and still argued over a thousand years later.

陈陶.b: Late Tang poet and recluse whose one great frontier quatrain is among the saddest war poems in Chinese.

poems.s: night desert moon cup horse flag
z: 葡萄美酒夜光杯，欲饮琵琶马上催。
醉卧沙场君莫笑，古来征战几人回？
e: Fine wine of grapes in cups of jade that glow at night;
We go to drink — the pipas urge us on from horseback, too.
If I lie drunk upon the sands, don't laugh at the sight:
Since ancient times, of those who went to war, how few came through?
poems.n: Grape wine and "night-shining cups" of white jade were exotic luxuries from Central Asia, and the pipa was the instrument of the steppe. The soldiers drink before battle; the last couplet is both bravado and despair.

poems.s: dusk sun mountains river tower
z: 白日依山尽，黄河入海流。
欲穷千里目，更上一层楼。
e: The white sun leans on the hills and is gone;
The Yellow River flows on to the sea.
If you would see a thousand li beyond,
Climb one more storey higher — and you'll see.
poems.n: Stork Tower in Puzhou (Shanxi) overlooked the Yellow River. The vast first couplet — the sun vanishing behind mountains, the river rolling to a sea a thousand miles away — leads to the most quoted lines of encouragement in Chinese: to see further, climb higher (更上一层楼), now said of any effort to do better.

poems.s: day clouds mountains fort river desert
z: 黄河远上白云间，一片孤城万仞山。
羌笛何须怨杨柳，春风不度玉门关。
e: Far up, the Yellow River climbs into white cloud;
One lonely fort amid the mountains, ten thousand fathoms tall.
Why must the Qiang flute play "Willows" and mourn aloud?
The spring wind never crosses Jade Gate Pass at all.
poems.n: Liangzhou (Gansu) on the north-western frontier. "Breaking Willows" was the farewell tune — but beyond the Jade Gate there is no spring and there are no willows, so the soldiers' homesickness has nowhere to go. Legend says Wang Zhihuan, Wang Changling and Gao Shi once bet on whose poems the singing girls of a tavern would sing; the loveliest girl sang this one.

poems.s: dawn spring rain petals birds cottage window
z: 春眠不觉晓，处处闻啼鸟。
夜来风雨声，花落知多少。
e: In spring I sleep and miss the break of day;
Everywhere I hear the birds sing on.
Last night, the sound of wind and rain —
How many blossoms fell before the dawn?
poems.n: After *Quiet Night Thoughts*, perhaps the most famous poem in Chinese. Half awake on a spring morning, the poet hears birdsong and remembers the night's storm: a moment of pure contentment shadowed by the thought of fallen petals — beauty and its passing in twenty characters.

poems.s: autumn hills cottage fields chrysanthemum two jar
z: 故人具鸡黍，邀我至田家。
绿树村边合，青山郭外斜。
开轩面场圃，把酒话桑麻。
待到重阳日，还来就菊花。
e: My old friend made a meal of chicken and millet,
And invited me to his farm to dine.
Green trees encircle the village;
Blue hills slope beyond the town line.
We open the window on the threshing yard and garden,
And over wine we talk of mulberry and hemp.
When the Double Ninth comes round again,
I'll come back for the chrysanthemums — I won't be exempt!
poems.n: The great pastoral poem of the Tang. Everything is plain — chicken and millet, talk of crops — and that is the joy. The promise to return on the Double Ninth, when people drank chrysanthemum wine, is the warmest possible thank-you.

poems.s: dusk moon river boat mist hills
z: 移舟泊烟渚，日暮客愁新。
野旷天低树，江清月近人。
e: I steer my boat to moor by a misty isle;
As the sun sets, a traveller's grief comes new.
The plain is vast — the sky stoops below the trees;
The river's clear — the moon comes close to me, too.
poems.n: Mooring at dusk on the Xin'an River in Zhejiang. The last two lines are among the most admired in Chinese: on the open plain the sky seems lower than the trees; in the clear river, the moon's reflection floats right beside the boat — the only companion the lonely traveller has.

poems.te: Gazing at Dongting Lake: To Chancellor Zhang
poems.s: autumn lake wall fisher boat mist
z: 八月湖水平，涵虚混太清。
气蒸云梦泽，波撼岳阳城。
欲济无舟楫，端居耻圣明。
坐观垂钓者，徒有羡鱼情。
e: In the eighth month, the lake brims level with its shore;
It holds the void, and merges with the sky.
Its vapours steam over the Yunmeng Marsh;
Its waves shake Yueyang's walls on high.
I'd cross, but have no boat or oar;
To sit idle in this age of sages would be shame.
I sit and watch the men who fish,
And only envy the fish they claim.
poems.n: A poem asking Zhang Jiuling, the chief minister, for an official post — but it is the first half that made it famous: the colossal lake in autumn flood, steaming over the marshes and shaking the city walls. The second half pleads, gracefully: "I'd cross over (into office) but have no boat; watching others fish, I can only envy their catch."

poems.s: winter mountains river person two
z: 人事有代谢，往来成古今。
江山留胜迹，我辈复登临。
水落鱼梁浅，天寒梦泽深。
羊公碑尚在，读罢泪沾襟。
e: Human affairs succeed each other, waxing and waning;
Comings and goings make up past and present.
The rivers and hills keep their famous sites,
And now we, in our turn, come climbing here.
The water has fallen — Fish Weir isle lies shallow;
The air is cold — the Yunmeng marsh lies deep.
Lord Yang's stone tablet still stands;
Reading it, we wet our robes and weep.
poems.n: Mount Xian near Xiangyang held a memorial stone to Yang Hu, a beloved 3rd-century governor who loved to climb it, and once said sadly that all the worthies who had climbed it were forgotten. People wept on reading his tablet, so it was called the "Tablet of Falling Tears". Meng Haoran, a native of Xiangyang, adds his own tears and his own reflection on time.

poems.te: Thinking of Xin the Elder in the South Pavilion on a Summer Day
poems.s: night summer moon lotus bamboo pavilion
z: 山光忽西落，池月渐东上。
散发乘夕凉，开轩卧闲敞。
荷风送香气，竹露滴清响。
欲取鸣琴弹，恨无知音赏。
感此怀故人，中宵劳梦想。
e: The mountain light drops suddenly into the west;
The pond-moon slowly rises in the east.
I loosen my hair to enjoy the evening cool,
And open the window, lying at ease, at least.
The lotus wind wafts its fragrance by;
Dew drips from bamboos with a crystal sound.
I'd like to take my zither down and play —
But there's no one who understands it around.
Moved by this, I think of my old friend,
And all night long, in dreams, I seek him out.
poems.n: A summer night so quiet that dew dripping from bamboo leaves is audible. The music he would play needs a 知音 — "one who knows the tone", the word for a true friend, from the story of Boya, who broke his zither when the only man who understood his music died.

poems.te: Returning to the Southern Hills at Year's End
poems.s: night winter moon pine window cottage
z: 北阙休上书，南山归敝庐。
不才明主弃，多病故人疏。
白发催年老，青阳逼岁除。
永怀愁不寐，松月夜窗虚。
e: No more petitions to the northern palace gate;
I'm going home to my poor hut in the southern hills.
Lacking talent, I'm cast off by our wise ruler;
Often sick, I'm left by old friends, as old age fills.
White hairs hurry my years toward age;
The green spring sun drives out the year at last.
Brooding long, I lie awake in sorrow —
Pine and moon, through the empty window, cast.
poems.n: Legend says that Meng Haoran was hiding in Wang Wei's office when the emperor walked in, and was made to recite a poem; he chose this one — and when the emperor heard "lacking talent, I'm cast off by our wise ruler", he said, "You never sought office; I never cast you off. Why slander me?" and sent him home. Whether true or not, it is a perfect story of a poet undone by a line.

poems.s: day cottage grass two person
z: 寂寂竟何待，朝朝空自归。
欲寻芳草去，惜与故人违。
当路谁相假，知音世所稀。
只应守寂寞，还掩故园扉。
e: In silence, what is it I'm waiting for?
Each day, I come home empty-handed, as before.
I want to go and seek the fragrant grass,
But hate to part from my old friend once more.
Those in power — who will lend me a hand?
True friends who understand are rare in the land.
I should keep to my solitude,
And close my old garden gate, as I'd planned.
poems.n: 737, after failing to win office in the capital. "Fragrant grass" is the hermit's life; Meng's only regret is leaving Wang Wei, the one man in Chang'an who truly understood him. The two were later painted together and are always named together as the masters of landscape verse.

poems.t: 宿业师山房期丁大不至
poems.te: Waiting in Vain for Ding the Elder at Master Ye's Mountain Lodge
poems.s: dusk moon pine mountains temple birds person
z: 夕阳度西岭，群壑倏已暝。
松月生夜凉，风泉满清听。
樵人归欲尽，烟鸟栖初定。
之子期宿来，孤琴候萝径。
e: The setting sun crosses the western ridge;
The valleys all have suddenly gone dark.
The moon through the pines brings the cool of night;
Wind and springs fill my ears, clear to hark.
The woodcutters have nearly all gone home;
In the mist, the birds have just settled to rest.
You promised to come and stay the night —
With my lone zither, I wait on the vine-hung path, your guest.
poems.n: A mountain evening described with exquisite precision, ending with the poet still waiting, zither in hand, for a friend who never comes. The disappointment is never stated.

poems.te: Climbing Orchid Mountain in Autumn: To Zhang the Fifth
poems.s: autumn dusk mountains geese river person clouds
z: 北山白云里，隐者自怡悦。
相望试登高，心随雁飞灭。
愁因薄暮起，兴是清秋发。
时见归村人，沙行渡头歇。
天边树若荠，江畔洲如月。
何当载酒来，共醉重阳节。
e: Among the white clouds of the northern hill,
A hermit finds his quiet joy.
To look for you I climb up high;
My heart flies with the geese, and fades away.
Sorrow rises with the gathering dusk;
Delight is born of the clear autumn day.
Now and then I see villagers going home,
Walking the sand, resting at the ferry's quay.
At the sky's edge, trees look small as shepherd's purse;
By the river, the islet curves like a moon.
When will you bring wine, so we can both
Get drunk on the Double Ninth, and soon?
poems.n: A climb to look toward a friend's home. The distant trees "like shepherd's-purse" (a tiny wild herb) and the sandbar "like the moon" give a precise sense of height and distance. The poem ends, as so often with Meng Haoran, with wine and the Double Ninth festival.

poems.te: Song of Returning to Deer Gate at Night
poems.s: night moon mountains pine temple river boat
z: 山寺钟鸣昼已昏，渔梁渡头争渡喧。
人随沙岸向江村，余亦乘舟归鹿门。
鹿门月照开烟树，忽到庞公栖隐处。
岩扉松径长寂寥，惟有幽人自来去。
e: The mountain temple's bell has rung; day has turned to dusk;
At Fish Weir ferry, people jostle, noisy, to cross.
The crowd goes off along the sandy bank toward the river villages;
I, too, take a boat back home to Deer Gate.
At Deer Gate, moonlight parts the misty trees;
Suddenly I'm at the place where Lord Pang lived hidden.
The rock door and the pine path are always silent —
Only the recluse comes and goes alone.
poems.n: Deer Gate Mountain near Xiangyang, where the Han-dynasty hermit Pang Degong refused all invitations to office and vanished into the hills gathering herbs. Meng Haoran retreated there too. The noisy crowd turns toward the villages; the poet alone turns toward silence.

poems.te: Early Cold on the River: Thoughts of Home
poems.s: autumn geese river sail leaves wind
z: 木落雁南度，北风江上寒。
我家襄水曲，遥隔楚云端。
乡泪客中尽，孤帆天际看。
迷津欲有问，平海夕漫漫。
e: Leaves fall; the wild geese cross toward the south;
The north wind blows; the river's growing cold.
My home is at a bend of the Xiang River,
Far off, beyond the clouds of Chu, I'm told.
My homesick tears are all used up in travel;
I watch a lonely sail at heaven's edge.
Lost, I'd ask the way to the ford —
But the sea-wide river spreads in the dusk past every ledge.
poems.n: Homesick on the lower Yangtze. "Asking the way to the ford" (问津) alludes to Confucius sending a disciple to ask two hermits for the ford — and being told, in effect, that the world was lost. Meng's way home, and his way in life, are both unclear.

poems.te: Seeing Zhu the Elder Off to Qin
poems.s: day rider two mountains wall
z: 游人五陵去，宝剑值千金。
分手脱相赠，平生一片心。
e: You're off to the Five Tombs, traveller;
My precious sword is worth a thousand gold.
At parting I take it off and give it to you —
With it, a whole life's loyal heart to hold.
poems.n: The Five Tombs (五陵) near Chang'an were where wealthy young knights lived. A sword was a gentleman's most treasured possession; giving it away meant giving one's heart. Twenty characters of gallant friendship.

poems.s: dusk desert snow fort horse geese
z: 白日登山望烽火，黄昏饮马傍交河。
行人刁斗风沙暗，公主琵琶幽怨多。
野云万里无城郭，雨雪纷纷连大漠。
胡雁哀鸣夜夜飞，胡儿眼泪双双落。
闻道玉门犹被遮，应将性命逐轻车。
年年战骨埋荒外，空见蒲桃入汉家。
e: By day we climb the hills to watch for beacon fires;
At dusk we water horses by the Jiao's cold tide.
The watch-gongs clang through the dark of wind and sand;
The princess's pipa sings of grief she cannot hide.
Wild clouds for ten thousand li, and not a town or wall;
Rain and snow come swirling down across the desert wide.
The northern geese cry mournfully, night after night they fly;
The Hu boys' tears fall down in pairs, and none can dry.
They say the Jade Gate's still shut against our coming home —
We must follow the light chariots, and stake our lives, and die.
Year after year, the bones of war are buried in the waste —
And all we get is grapes, brought into the Han to taste.
poems.n: An "old" frontier song, set in the Han but aimed at Xuanzong's wars. The princess's pipa recalls the Han princess married off to a Central Asian king, who played her grief on the pipa. When Emperor Wu of Han's army failed against Ferghana, he shut the Jade Gate and forbade the soldiers to return; the only gain from all the dead was the grapevine, brought back to China. The last line is one of the bitterest in Tang poetry.

poems.s: night moon fort mountains flag
z: 秦时明月汉时关，万里长征人未还。
但使龙城飞将在，不教胡马度阴山。
e: The moon of Qin, the passes of the Han —
Ten thousand li they marched; not one man has come back.
If only the Flying General of Dragon City were alive,
No Hu horse would cross the Yin Hills to attack.
poems.n: "Qin moon, Han passes": the same moon and the same forts have watched a thousand years of frontier war — the whole of history in one line. The Flying General was Li Guang of the Han, whom the Xiongnu feared above all others. Often called the finest quatrain of the Tang.

poems.s: snow mountains clouds fort desert flag
z: 青海长云暗雪山，孤城遥望玉门关。
黄沙百战穿金甲，不破楼兰终不还。
e: Long clouds over Qinghai darken the snowy peaks;
From the lone fort I gaze toward Jade Gate, far away.
A hundred battles in the yellow sand have worn our armour through —
Until we've crushed Loulan, we'll never go home; we'll stay.
poems.n: Qinghai Lake, the snow-capped Qilian range and the Jade Gate Pass trace the whole north-western frontier of the Tang. The soldiers' oath in the last line — 不破楼兰终不还 — is still quoted as a vow of total resolve.

poems.s: dusk desert wind flag rider fort
z: 大漠风尘日色昏，红旗半卷出辕门。
前军夜战洮河北，已报生擒吐谷浑。
e: Across the great desert, wind and dust have dimmed the sun;
Red banners half-furled, they ride out through the camp's gate.
The vanguard fought by night north of the Tao — and won:
The Tuyuhun chief's been taken alive — the news can't wait!
poems.n: A burst of victory: the reinforcements are still marching into the dust storm when word arrives that the vanguard has already won. The Tuyuhun were a nomadic kingdom around Qinghai.

poems.te: Seeing Xin Jian Off at Lotus Tower
poems.s: dawn rain river tower mountains boat
z: 寒雨连江夜入吴，平明送客楚山孤。
洛阳亲友如相问，一片冰心在玉壶。
e: Cold rain spread over the river as night came into Wu;
At dawn I see you off; the hills of Chu stand lone.
If kin and friends in Luoyang ask about me, tell them true:
"A heart of ice in a pot of jade" — that's all I own.
poems.n: Wang Changling, slandered and demoted, sees a friend off to Luoyang from the Lotus Tower at Zhenjiang. 一片冰心在玉壶 — a heart pure as ice in a jade vessel, unchanged by slander — became an idiom for integrity.

poems.s: spring willow tower person
z: 闺中少妇不知愁，春日凝妆上翠楼。
忽见陌头杨柳色，悔教夫婿觅封侯。
e: The young wife in her chamber doesn't know what sorrow is;
One spring day, all made up, she climbs the jade-green tower.
She suddenly sees the green of the willows along the road —
And rues the day she sent her man to seek a lordship's power.
poems.n: A masterpiece of the sudden turn. The willows by the road — the trees of parting — make her realise in an instant what she gave up when she encouraged her husband to win a title (封侯) at the frontier.

poems.s: summer lotus lake boat person
z: 荷叶罗裙一色裁，芙蓉向脸两边开。
乱入池中看不见，闻歌始觉有人来。
e: Lotus leaves and silken skirt are cut from the same green;
Lotus blooms beside her face unfold on either side.
Lost amid the pond, she cannot now be seen —
Until a song rings out, and you know where she hides.
poems.n: The girl is so like the lotus — green skirt, pink cheeks — that she vanishes among the flowers; only her song gives her away.

poems.s: dawn autumn palace crows person
z: 奉帚平明金殿开，暂将团扇共徘徊。
玉颜不及寒鸦色，犹带昭阳日影来。
e: At dawn, with broom in hand, she waits for the golden hall to open,
And lingers for a while beside her round silk fan.
Her jade-white face is worth less than a crow's black feathers —
For the crows still bring the sunlight of Zhaoyang, as only they can.
poems.n: Lady Ban, a virtuous Han consort, was displaced by the dancer Zhao Feiyan and withdrew to the Changxin Palace to serve the Empress Dowager. She once compared herself to a fan, discarded when autumn comes. Here her beauty is worth less than the black crows — who at least fly from Zhaoyang Palace, where the emperor is, with its sunshine (his favour) on their wings.

poems.s: dusk autumn tower fort sun wind
z: 烽火城西百尺楼，黄昏独上海风秋。
更吹羌笛关山月，无那金闺万里愁。
e: West of the beacon-fire city stands a hundred-foot tower;
At dusk I climb it alone; autumn wind blows off the sea.
Then a Qiang flute plays "Moon over the Mountain Pass" — what power
Can ease her grief ten thousand li away, in her golden room, for me?
poems.n: A soldier on the tower at dusk hears a flute playing a frontier song of homesickness — and thinks not of his own grief but of his wife's, far away, which he can do nothing to relieve. The "sea" is Qinghai Lake.

poems.s: night moon mountains river boat two
z: 沅水通波接武冈，送君不觉有离伤。
青山一道同云雨，明月何曾是两乡。
e: The Yuan's waves flow straight on to Wugang;
Seeing you off, I hardly feel the parting's pain.
One range of green hills shares the same clouds and rain —
And when was the bright moon in two lands? It shines on both the same.
poems.n: A rare cheerful farewell, written in exile at Longbiao: the same river, the same hills, the same weather and the same moon join the friends, so they are never really apart.

poems.s: night moon window frost
z: 床前明月光，疑是地上霜。
举头望明月，低头思故乡。
e: Before my bed there gleams a silver light —
Could it be frost that settles on the ground?
I raise my head: the moon is shining bright;
I bow my head: my thoughts are homeward bound.
poems.n: The best-known poem in the Chinese language; nearly every child can recite it. Far from home, the traveller wakes to moonlight so pale he takes it for frost. The same moon shines over his distant hometown, and the simple movement of raising and lowering his head carries him there. (床 may be a bed, or — some scholars argue — the railing of a well in the courtyard.)

poems.te: Viewing the Waterfall at Mount Lu
poems.s: day sun peaks waterfall mist
z: 日照香炉生紫烟，遥看瀑布挂前川。
飞流直下三千尺，疑是银河落九天。
e: Sunlight on Censer Peak sets violet mist aglow;
Far off, a waterfall hangs on the stream below.
It flies three thousand feet straight down through air —
The Milky Way, it seems, poured from the Ninth Heaven there.
poems.n: Censer Peak (香炉峰) on Mount Lu in Jiangxi is named for its shape and the incense-like mists that rise from it. "Three thousand feet" is Li Bai's typical grand exaggeration. The Chinese call the Milky Way the "Silver River" (银河), and the Ninth Heaven is the highest of the heavens — so the waterfall becomes the river of stars tumbling to earth.

poems.s: dawn clouds peaks river boat
z: 朝辞白帝彩云间，千里江陵一日还。
两岸猿声啼不住，轻舟已过万重山。
e: At dawn I leave White Emperor town, high in the rosy cloud;
A thousand li to Jiangling — and home within a day.
From both the banks the gibbons cry, unceasing and aloud;
My little boat has slipped ten thousand peaks away.
poems.n: Written in 759. Li Bai, exiled to the far southwest for his part in a prince's rebellion, received a pardon at Baidi, high above the Yangtze. The headlong rush down the Three Gorges mirrors his joy: the boat is "light" (轻舟) in more ways than one, and the gibbons' cries — usually the saddest sound in Chinese poetry — are left behind.

poems.t: 黄鹤楼送孟浩然之广陵
poems.te: Seeing Meng Haoran Off to Guangling at Yellow Crane Tower
poems.s: spring tower river sail willow
z: 故人西辞黄鹤楼，烟花三月下扬州。
孤帆远影碧空尽，唯见长江天际流。
e: My old friend bids the Yellow Crane Tower in the west goodbye;
In the third month's mist of blossom, down to Yangzhou he goes.
His lonely sail, a fading shade, is lost in the blue sky;
Now only the Long River to the edge of heaven flows.
poems.n: Meng Haoran, twelve years older, was a poet Li Bai idolised. The poem names no feeling at all — Li Bai simply stands watching until the sail vanishes, and that long gaze is the friendship. Yangzhou (Guangling) in spring was the most glamorous city of the empire; 烟花 "mist and flowers" became a set phrase for its springtime.

poems.s: spring river boat peach two
z: 李白乘舟将欲行，忽闻岸上踏歌声。
桃花潭水深千尺，不及汪伦送我情。
e: I, Li Bai, am aboard my boat, about to sail away,
When suddenly from shore I hear a stamping, singing throng.
Though Peach Blossom Pool is a thousand feet deep, they say,
It's not so deep as Wang Lun's love that sees me off with song.
poems.n: Wang Lun was a local gentleman of Jingxian (Anhui) who had invited the famous poet to stay. As Li Bai was leaving, Wang came down to the shore with villagers, singing and stamping out the rhythm (踏歌, "stepping song"). Naming himself in the first line is a cheerful informality almost unique in Tang poetry.

poems.s: night moon flowers person jar cup
z: 花间一壶酒，独酌无相亲。
举杯邀明月，对影成三人。
月既不解饮，影徒随我身。
暂伴月将影，行乐须及春。
我歌月徘徊，我舞影零乱。
醒时同交欢，醉后各分散。
永结无情游，相期邈云汉。
e: Among the flowers, a jug of wine;
I pour alone, with no one nigh.
I lift my cup to invite the moon —
With my shadow, we make three: moon, shade and I.
But the moon has never learned to drink,
And my shadow only does what I do;
Yet for a while, with moon and shadow,
Let's revel while the spring is new.
I sing — the moon lingers and sways;
I dance — my shadow reels and sprawls.
Sober, we share our joy together;
Drunk, we each go where slumber calls.
Let us pledge a friendship free of worldly ties,
To meet again beyond the Milky Way's far skies.
poems.n: The first of Li Bai's four poems "Drinking Alone by Moonlight". Loneliness becomes a party of three, then dissolves back into solitude. The closing pledge of a 无情游 — a companionship beyond human feeling, with moon and shadow who have none — to be renewed in the Milky Way (云汉), makes his two silent friends his companions for eternity.

poems.s: night moon river mountains cup jar two
z: 君不见黄河之水天上来，奔流到海不复回。
君不见高堂明镜悲白发，朝如青丝暮成雪。
人生得意须尽欢，莫使金樽空对月。
天生我材必有用，千金散尽还复来。
烹羊宰牛且为乐，会须一饮三百杯。
岑夫子，丹丘生，将进酒，杯莫停。
与君歌一曲，请君为我倾耳听。
钟鼓馔玉不足贵，但愿长醉不复醒。
古来圣贤皆寂寞，惟有饮者留其名。
陈王昔时宴平乐，斗酒十千恣欢谑。
主人何为言少钱，径须沽取对君酌。
五花马，千金裘，呼儿将出换美酒，与尔同销万古愁。
e: Have you not seen the Yellow River's waters, sent from heaven's height,
Rush to the sea and never more return?
Have you not seen, in lofty halls, the mirror mourn hair turned to white —
Black silk at dawn, by dusk like snow? Then learn:
When life goes well, enjoy it to the full;
Don't let your golden goblet face the moon in vain.
Heaven made my talents — they will find their use;
Spend a thousand gold — the gold will come again.
Roast the lamb and kill the ox, and let us make merry —
Three hundred cups at a single sitting we must drain!
Master Cen, and Danqiu, my friend,
Bring in the wine — don't let your cups stand still!
Let me sing a song for you —
Lend me your ears, if you will:
Bells and drums and jade-fine feasts — what are they worth?
I only wish to stay drunk, and never wake again.
The sages and the worthies all lie lonely in the earth;
Only the great drinkers' names remain.
The Prince of Chen once feasted in the Pingle Hall,
Ten thousand cash a cask, carousing without end.
Why does our host say he is short of money? Go and buy it all,
And fill our cups, so we can drink, my friend!
My dappled horse,
My fur worth a thousand gold —
Call the boy, take them out, and trade them for fine wine,
And with you I'll drown the sorrows of ten thousand years untold!
poems.n: "Bring in the Wine" (an old Han ballad title) was written around 752 as Li Bai drank with his friends Cen Xun and Yuan Danqiu. It opens with two images of time's unstoppable flow — the Yellow River pouring from heaven to the sea, hair turning white in a single day — and answers them with defiant joy and boundless self-belief. The Prince of Chen is the poet Cao Zhi, famous for his lavish banquets at Pingle Lodge.

poems.te: The Road to Shu Is Hard
poems.s: day peaks clouds pine waterfall mist birds
z: 噫吁嚱，危乎高哉！
蜀道之难，难于上青天！
蚕丛及鱼凫，开国何茫然！
尔来四万八千岁，不与秦塞通人烟。
西当太白有鸟道，可以横绝峨眉巅。
地崩山摧壮士死，然后天梯石栈相钩连。
上有六龙回日之高标，下有冲波逆折之回川。
黄鹤之飞尚不得过，猿猱欲度愁攀援。
青泥何盘盘，百步九折萦岩峦。
扪参历井仰胁息，以手抚膺坐长叹。
问君西游何时还？畏途巉岩不可攀。
但见悲鸟号古木，雄飞雌从绕林间。
又闻子规啼夜月，愁空山。
蜀道之难，难于上青天，使人听此凋朱颜！
连峰去天不盈尺，枯松倒挂倚绝壁。
飞湍瀑流争喧豗，砯崖转石万壑雷。
其险也如此，嗟尔远道之人胡为乎来哉！
剑阁峥嵘而崔嵬，一夫当关，万夫莫开。
所守或匪亲，化为狼与豺。
朝避猛虎，夕避长蛇；磨牙吮血，杀人如麻。
锦城虽云乐，不如早还家。
蜀道之难，难于上青天，侧身西望长咨嗟！
e: Ah! Oh! How steep! How high!
The road to Shu is hard — harder than climbing the blue sky!
Cancong and Yufu, who founded the land —
How dim and distant, those days, to understand!
For forty-eight thousand years since then,
No smoke of hearths crossed to the Qin frontier's men.
West, by Mount Taibai, runs a track only birds can trace,
That cuts across to Emei's summit face.
Then the earth split, the mountain fell, the strong men died,
And ladders to heaven, stone plank-roads, were linked along the side.
Above, a peak so high the sun's six dragons turn their car;
Below, the rapids dash and twist where the whirling eddies are.
The yellow crane in flight can never cross that height;
The gibbons long to pass, and dread the climb outright.
How Green Mud Ridge goes coiling, coiling round —
Nine turns in a hundred steps, through crags it's wound!
You touch Orion, pass the Well Star, gasp and look on high;
You sit and clutch your chest, and heave a long, long sigh.
I ask you, traveller to the west, when will you come back home?
The road is fearful, sheer the cliffs — no foot can overcome.
You see only mournful birds that cry in ancient trees,
The male in front, the female after, circling through the leaves;
You hear the cuckoo weep beneath the moon at night,
Grieving the empty hills.
The road to Shu is hard — harder than climbing the blue sky!
Just hearing of it, rosy cheeks would fade and youth would fly.
Peak after peak, not a foot from heaven's floor,
Dead pines hang upside down from cliffs they cling to more and more.
The flying torrents, roaring falls, compete in their uproar;
They pound the cliffs and roll the rocks — ten thousand gorges' thunder-roar.
Such is its peril!
Alas, you traveller from afar, why ever come this way?
Sword Gate Pass looms, jagged and steep:
One man can hold it — ten thousand cannot break in to sweep.
And if its guards are not men you can trust,
They'll turn to wolves and jackals, as such men must.
By day beware the tiger, by night beware the snake —
They grind their teeth and suck men's blood, and kill like reapers' rake.
Though Brocade City may be fair, they say,
Better go home without delay.
The road to Shu is hard — harder than climbing the blue sky!
I turn and gaze toward the west, and heave a long, long sigh.
poems.n: Shu is today's Sichuan, cut off from the central plain by mountain ranges crossed only on plank roads pinned to cliff faces. Li Bai, a son of Shu, mixes legend (the ancient kings Cancong and Yufu; five strongmen killed when a mountain collapsed as they dragged a snake from its cave; the six dragons pulling the sun's chariot) with real geography, in wildly irregular lines that lurch like the road itself. When He Zhizhang read it, he called Li Bai "an immortal banished from heaven".

poems.s: winter snow mountains river sail person
z: 金樽清酒斗十千，玉盘珍羞直万钱。
停杯投箸不能食，拔剑四顾心茫然。
欲渡黄河冰塞川，将登太行雪满山。
闲来垂钓碧溪上，忽复乘舟梦日边。
行路难，行路难，多歧路，今安在？
长风破浪会有时，直挂云帆济沧海。
e: Clear wine in cups of gold, ten thousand cash a measure;
Rare dishes on a plate of jade, worth ten thousand more —
I set my cup aside, cast down my chopsticks — no pleasure;
I draw my sword and look around, heart lost, unsure.
I'd cross the Yellow River — ice has choked its flow;
I'd climb the Taihang Mountains — snow lies deep on every height.
Then let me fish, as the old sage did, where green brooks go,
Or dream, like Yi Yin, of sailing toward the sun's own light.
Hard is the road! Hard is the road!
So many forks — and where am I now?
A day will come to ride the wind and break the waves:
I'll hoist my cloud-high sail and cross the boundless sea somehow.
poems.n: Written in 744 when Li Bai left the court at Chang'an, his hopes of a political career in ruins. Ice and snow block every way forward. The fisherman is Lü Shang, who fished in obscurity until King Wen of Zhou discovered him; Yi Yin dreamed of sailing past the sun just before King Tang employed him — both sages who waited for their moment. The famous last couplet turns despair into confidence.

poems.s: day sun mountains river sail
z: 天门中断楚江开，碧水东流至此回。
两岸青山相对出，孤帆一片日边来。
e: The Gate of Heaven splits in two; the Chu River bursts through;
Its blue-green waters, flowing east, here swirl and turn around.
From either bank the green hills stride out, facing, into view —
And from beside the sun there comes a single sail, without a sound.
poems.n: Tianmen ("Heaven's Gate") is a pair of hills facing each other across the Yangtze in Anhui. Sailing downstream, Li Bai sees the hills seem to step forward to meet him as his boat approaches — a moving-camera view, a thousand years before cinema.

poems.s: day mountains clouds birds person pine
z: 众鸟高飞尽，孤云独去闲。
相看两不厌，只有敬亭山。
e: The flocks of birds fly high and disappear;
A lonely cloud drifts off without a care.
We gaze and gaze, and never tire of it —
Just Jingting Mountain, and I, sitting there.
poems.n: Written in 753 near Xuancheng, when Li Bai was past fifty and long out of favour. Birds and clouds — like friends and fortune — all leave him; only the mountain stays, and the two regard each other like old friends who need no words.

poems.te: Staying the Night at a Mountain Temple
poems.s: night stars temple mountains crescent
z: 危楼高百尺，手可摘星辰。
不敢高声语，恐惊天上人。
e: The towering pagoda soars a hundred feet in height;
From here my hand could pluck the stars of night.
I dare not raise my voice above a sigh,
For fear of waking those who dwell on high.
poems.n: A temple tower on a mountaintop, so high that the stars are within reach and heaven's residents might overhear. Built entirely from playful exaggeration, it is one of the first poems Chinese children learn.

poems.te: Song of the Moon over Mount Emei
poems.s: night autumn crescent mountains river boat
z: 峨眉山月半轮秋，影入平羌江水流。
夜发清溪向三峡，思君不见下渝州。
e: Over Mount Emei hangs the autumn half-moon's light;
Its image floats along the Pingqiang's flowing stream.
I leave Clear Creek for the Three Gorges in the night;
I miss you — you are lost to sight — and drift to Yuzhou in a dream.
poems.n: Written around 725 when the young Li Bai first left his home province of Shu. In four lines he names five places — Emei, the Pingqiang River, Clear Creek, the Three Gorges, Yuzhou — yet the poem reads as one smooth glide downstream. The "you" he misses may be the moon itself, hidden now behind the gorge cliffs, or a friend left behind.

poems.te: Hearing a Flute on a Spring Night in Luoyang
poems.s: night spring moon willow tower
z: 谁家玉笛暗飞声，散入春风满洛城。
此夜曲中闻折柳，何人不起故园情。
e: Whose jade flute sends its notes in secret flight,
Scattered by spring winds through Luoyang's every street?
Hearing "Breaking Willows" in the tune tonight,
Whose heart would not for home and garden beat?
poems.n: "Breaking Willows" (折杨柳) was a farewell tune: friends parting gave each other a willow twig, because 柳 (willow) sounds like 留 (stay). Hearing it played by an unseen flautist in the spring night, the poet realises the whole city must be thinking of home.

poems.s: dusk sun hills river wall rider two
z: 青山横北郭，白水绕东城。
此地一为别，孤蓬万里征。
浮云游子意，落日故人情。
挥手自兹去，萧萧班马鸣。
e: Green hills lie stretched beyond the northern wall;
White water winds around the eastern town.
Once we have parted here, you'll be a lonely weed
Ten thousand li along the road, wind-blown.
The drifting clouds — a wanderer's mind;
The setting sun — an old friend's heart.
We wave our hands, and from this place you go;
Your horse, leaving the herd, neighs as we part.
poems.n: A model regulated poem, its middle couplets perfectly parallel. The drifting cloud is the departing friend, the reluctant setting sun the friend left behind. The last line borrows from the *Book of Songs*: 班马 is a horse separated from its companions, crying out — the animals feel the parting too.

poems.s: night moon clouds river boat hills
z: 渡远荆门外，来从楚国游。
山随平野尽，江入大荒流。
月下飞天镜，云生结海楼。
仍怜故乡水，万里送行舟。
e: I've crossed afar, beyond the Jingmen Gate,
To roam among the lands of ancient Chu.
The hills give way as the broad plains begin;
The River pours into the wilds — a boundless view.
The moon drops down, a mirror flying through the sky;
Clouds rise and build sea-towers out of the blue.
Still I love my native river, that has come
Ten thousand li to see my boat off, as friends do.
poems.n: Li Bai at about twenty-four, leaving Sichuan for the first time. Past the Jingmen gorge the mountains suddenly end and the Yangtze spreads into the plains of Hubei. The moon in the water is a "flying mirror", the clouds a mirage of "sea towers". The "farewell" of the title is the river from home seeing him off.

poems.t: 闻王昌龄左迁龙标遥有此寄
poems.te: On Hearing That Wang Changling Was Demoted to Longbiao
poems.s: night moon willow mountains river
z: 杨花落尽子规啼，闻道龙标过五溪。
我寄愁心与明月，随君直到夜郎西。
e: The willow-down has fallen, and the cuckoos weep;
I hear you pass Five Streams, to Longbiao sent away.
I give my grieving heart into the bright moon's keep,
To follow you to the west of Yelang all the way.
poems.n: Wang Changling, a fellow poet and friend, was banished to remote Longbiao (in today's Hunan) around 748. The cuckoo's cry was heard as 不如归去, "better go home". Unable to follow, Li Bai entrusts his heart to the moon, which shines on both of them — one of the best-loved images of friendship in Chinese.

poems.s: night spring moon palace flowers clouds
z: 云想衣裳花想容，春风拂槛露华浓。
若非群玉山头见，会向瑶台月下逢。
e: Clouds bring her robes to mind, and flowers, her face;
The spring wind strokes the rail, the dew lies thick and bright.
If she is not a goddess seen on Jade Mountain's height,
She must be one you'd meet on Jasper Terrace by moonlight.
poems.n: Written to order around 743, when Emperor Xuanzong and his beloved Consort Yang were admiring peonies at the Aloeswood Pavilion. Li Bai, reportedly still drunk, dashed off three songs. In this one the consort and the peony blur into each other, and both into a goddess of the Queen Mother of the West's paradise (Jade Mountain, Jasper Terrace).

poems.s: night autumn moon wall wind
z: 长安一片月，万户捣衣声。
秋风吹不尽，总是玉关情。
何日平胡虏，良人罢远征。
e: One sheet of moonlight over Chang'an lies;
From ten thousand homes the fulling-mallets pound.
The autumn wind blows on and never dies —
All of it heartache, for the Jade Gate bound.
When will we crush the raiders and have peace,
So my good man's long campaigns may cease?
poems.n: Women beat cloth on stones to soften it before sewing winter clothes for husbands at the frontier, so the sound of "pounding clothes" (捣衣) was the sound of autumn longing. The Jade Gate Pass (玉门关) was the gateway to the western frontier. Li Bai turns an old southern love-song form into the voice of a whole city's grief.

poems.te: The Moon over the Mountain Pass
poems.s: night moon clouds mountains fort wind
z: 明月出天山，苍茫云海间。
长风几万里，吹度玉门关。
汉下白登道，胡窥青海湾。
由来征战地，不见有人还。
戍客望边色，思归多苦颜。
高楼当此夜，叹息未应闲。
e: The bright moon rises over Tianshan's height,
Amid a boundless sea of clouds and haze.
A long wind sweeps ten thousand li of night,
And blows through Jade Gate Pass along its ways.
Han armies marched down Baideng's road;
The Hu still eye the bays of Qinghai's shore.
From these old battlefields, as all men know,
Not one has ever come back home from war.
The soldiers gaze upon the frontier scene,
Their faces bitter, longing to return;
In high towers on this night, their wives, unseen,
Must sigh and sigh, and cannot rest, but yearn.
poems.n: An old ballad title, reworked on an immense scale: the moon over the Tianshan range, a wind blowing ten thousand li to the Jade Gate. Baideng is where the Han founder was besieged by the Xiongnu; Qinghai Lake was a Tang–Tibetan battleground. The last couplet cuts from the frontier to the wives in their towers far away, watching the same moon.

poems.s: night autumn moon palace window
z: 玉阶生白露，夜久侵罗袜。
却下水晶帘，玲珑望秋月。
e: White dew is forming on the jade stair;
The night grows long; it soaks her silken hose.
She lowers the crystal curtain — there,
Through its glinting beads, the autumn moon still glows.
poems.n: A palace lament in which nothing is said of feeling. A woman has waited on the steps so long that the dew soaks her stockings; she goes in and lowers the blind — and still cannot stop gazing at the moon through it. Ezra Pound admired the poem for saying everything by implication.

poems.s: day window palace flowers
z: 美人卷珠帘，深坐颦蛾眉。
但见泪痕湿，不知心恨谁。
e: The beauty rolls the pearly curtain high,
Sits deep within, her moth-brows knit in pain.
You only see the tear-stains, not yet dry —
But whom her heart resents, she won't explain.
poems.n: Another portrait of a woman's sorrow told only through gesture: rolling up the blind (to watch for someone), sitting long, frowning, weeping. "Moth-brows" — long, curved, delicate eyebrows — were the classic mark of beauty. The cause is left a mystery.

poems.t: 宣州谢朓楼饯别校书叔云
poems.te: Farewell to Secretary Shuyun at Xie Tiao's Tower in Xuanzhou
poems.s: autumn day geese tower river mountains wind
z: 弃我去者，昨日之日不可留；
乱我心者，今日之日多烦忧。
长风万里送秋雁，对此可以酣高楼。
蓬莱文章建安骨，中间小谢又清发。
俱怀逸兴壮思飞，欲上青天揽明月。
抽刀断水水更流，举杯销愁愁更愁。
人生在世不称意，明朝散发弄扁舟。
e: What has abandoned me —
Yesterday — I cannot keep;
What troubles my heart —
Today — its cares are deep.
The long wind speeds the autumn geese ten thousand li away;
Facing this, in the high tower, let us drink our fill today.
Your prose has Penglai's grace, my verse the bones of Jian'an's age,
With Little Xie's clear freshness in between, upon the page.
We both are full of soaring moods and thoughts in lofty flight —
We'd climb the azure sky to pluck the moon so bright.
I draw my sword to cut the stream — the stream flows on the more;
I raise my cup to drown my grief — my grief grows all the more.
If life in this world will not go the way we planned,
Tomorrow, hair unpinned, I'll take a skiff and leave the land.
poems.n: Xie Tiao (464–499), a poet Li Bai revered, built this tower in Xuanzhou. "Penglai writing" alludes to the Han imperial library, "Jian'an bones" to the vigour of Cao Cao's era — praise for his kinsman's prose and his own verse. "Cutting water with a sword" became a proverb for sorrow that cannot be stopped; unpinning the hair meant leaving official life for a free one.

poems.te: A Dream Journey to Mount Tianmu: A Farewell
poems.s: night moon peaks clouds waterfall lake mist crane
z: 海客谈瀛洲，烟涛微茫信难求；
越人语天姥，云霞明灭或可睹。
天姥连天向天横，势拔五岳掩赤城。
天台四万八千丈，对此欲倒东南倾。
我欲因之梦吴越，一夜飞度镜湖月。
湖月照我影，送我至剡溪。
谢公宿处今尚在，渌水荡漾清猿啼。
脚著谢公屐，身登青云梯。
半壁见海日，空中闻天鸡。
千岩万转路不定，迷花倚石忽已暝。
熊咆龙吟殷岩泉，栗深林兮惊层巅。
云青青兮欲雨，水澹澹兮生烟。
列缺霹雳，丘峦崩摧。
洞天石扉，訇然中开。
青冥浩荡不见底，日月照耀金银台。
霓为衣兮风为马，云之君兮纷纷而来下。
虎鼓瑟兮鸾回车，仙之人兮列如麻。
忽魂悸以魄动，恍惊起而长嗟。
惟觉时之枕席，失向来之烟霞。
世间行乐亦如此，古来万事东流水。
别君去兮何时还？且放白鹿青崖间，须行即骑访名山。
安能摧眉折腰事权贵，使我不得开心颜！
e: Seafarers tell of Yingzhou, isle of the immortals' rest —
Through misty waves so dim and far, it's truly hard to find;
But men of Yue speak of Mount Tianmu, whose crest
In flickering cloud and rosy light may sometimes be divined.
Tianmu joins the sky and lies across the sky's expanse;
It overtops the Five Great Peaks and hides the Red Wall Hill;
Tiantai, forty-eight thousand feet, at a single glance
Seems to topple southeast before it, bowing lower still.
So, longing for Wu and Yue, I dreamed — and in one night
Flew over Mirror Lake beneath the moon.
The lake-moon lit my shadow, and it led me with its light
To Shan Creek, where Lord Xie once lodged; it stands there still,
With clear green waters rippling, and the gibbons' crying shrill.
I put on Lord Xie's climbing clogs
And mounted the ladder of blue cloud.
Halfway up the cliff I saw the sun rise from the sea,
And heard the Heavenly Rooster crow aloud.
A thousand crags, ten thousand turns — the path would twist and stray;
Lost among flowers, leaning on rocks, I found the light had gone away.
Bears roared and dragons chanted, booming through the rocks and springs;
The deep woods shook, the topmost peaks were startled at such things.
The clouds were dark and heavy, close to rain;
The waters rippled, breathing mist again.
Then lightning split the sky, and thunder roared;
The hills and ridges crumbled and collapsed.
The stone gates of the grotto-heaven
With a crash flew open wide.
A blue void, vast and fathomless, lay beyond;
Sun and moon shone on terraces of gold and silver inside.
With rainbows for their robes and winds for horses,
The Lords of the Clouds came streaming down in throngs;
Tigers struck the zithers, phoenixes drew the carriages round;
Immortals stood in ranks, as thick as hemp upon the ground.
Then suddenly my soul was shaken, my spirit stirred —
I started up awake with a long sigh;
There was only the pillow and the mat I woke upon;
The mist and rosy clouds of before were gone.
The pleasures of this world are just the same:
Since ancient times, all things flow east like water, and are gone.
I leave you now — when shall I return?
For now I'll set my white deer free among the green cliffs to roam,
And ride it, when I must, to visit the famous mountains, my true home.
How could I bow my brows and bend my back to serve the great,
And never let my heart be glad, and never let my face be bright?
poems.n: Written in 745 as Li Bai left eastern Shandong for the south, a year after leaving the court. The dream climbs Mount Tianmu in Zhejiang in the footsteps of Xie Lingyun (Lord Xie), the 5th-century landscape poet who invented special clogs for mountain climbing, and bursts into a vision of an immortals' paradise — which vanishes on waking. The moral explodes in the last line: no worldly glory is worth bending the back to the powerful. It became a creed for independent spirits.

poems.s: day clouds tower river hills sail
z: 凤凰台上凤凰游，凤去台空江自流。
吴宫花草埋幽径，晋代衣冠成古丘。
三山半落青天外，二水中分白鹭洲。
总为浮云能蔽日，长安不见使人愁。
e: On Phoenix Terrace phoenixes once used to play;
The phoenixes are gone, the terrace bare; the river flows its way.
The flowers and grasses of the Wu palace bury hidden lanes;
The robes and caps of Jin are ancient mounds today.
The Three Peaks, half-dissolving, lean beyond the blue;
Two waters split around White Egret Isle midway.
It's all because the drifting clouds can hide the sun —
Chang'an is lost to sight, and grief has come to stay.
poems.n: Jinling (Nanjing) had been the capital of six dynasties, all long vanished. Li Bai's poem deliberately echoes Cui Hao's *Yellow Crane Tower*, which he had admired. The ending turns from history to politics: the "drifting clouds" hiding the sun are the slanderers who cut Li Bai off from the emperor in Chang'an.

poems.s: autumn river person mountains window
z: 白发三千丈，缘愁似个长。
不知明镜里，何处得秋霜。
e: My white hair hangs three thousand yards —
So long, because my grief is long as well.
Into the bright mirror I stare:
Where did this autumn frost come from? I cannot tell.
poems.n: From a series of seventeen songs on the Qiupu River in Anhui, written in Li Bai's fifties. "White hair three thousand *zhang*" (about 10 km!) is the most famous exaggeration in Chinese poetry, and it is somehow perfectly true to the feeling of seeing oneself suddenly old.

poems.s: dusk sun cup jar person cottage
z: 兰陵美酒郁金香，玉碗盛来琥珀光。
但使主人能醉客，不知何处是他乡。
e: The fine wine of Lanling breathes of turmeric's scent;
Poured in a bowl of jade, it gleams with amber light.
If only my host can get his guest well drunk tonight,
I'll never know which land is foreign, or where I went.
poems.n: Lanling (in Shandong) was famous for its wine, scented with 郁金 (turmeric or curcuma). Most travel poems are homesick; this one, from Li Bai's carefree younger days, cheerfully proposes that good enough wine makes anywhere home.

poems.s: dusk palace birds flowers person
z: 越王勾践破吴归，义士还家尽锦衣。
宫女如花满春殿，只今惟有鹧鸪飞。
e: King Goujian of Yue came home, the land of Wu destroyed;
His loyal warriors returned, all dressed in brocade.
Palace girls, like flowers, filled the spring halls he enjoyed —
And now, there's only partridges flying where they played.
poems.n: Goujian, king of Yue, was crushed by Wu, slept on brushwood and tasted gall for years to keep his vengeance alive, and finally destroyed Wu in 473 BC. Three lines of triumph and splendour; then one line of desolation sweeps it all away.

poems.te: Question and Answer in the Mountains
poems.s: spring peaks river petals peach person
z: 问余何意栖碧山，笑而不答心自闲。
桃花流水窅然去，别有天地非人间。
e: You ask me why I dwell among the green hills here;
I smile and don't reply — my heart is calm and free.
Peach blossoms on the water drift away, and disappear:
There is another world, not of men, for me.
poems.n: Peach blossoms floating on a stream recall Tao Yuanming's *Peach Blossom Spring*, a hidden paradise found by following petals upstream. The best answer to "why live in the mountains?" is a smile.

poems.te: Drinking with a Recluse in the Mountains
poems.s: spring mountains flowers two cup jar
z: 两人对酌山花开，一杯一杯复一杯。
我醉欲眠卿且去，明朝有意抱琴来。
e: We two sit drinking where the mountain flowers bloom —
One cup, another cup, and then another cup.
I'm drunk and want to sleep — be off now, leave the room!
Tomorrow, if you like, bring your zither, and come up.
poems.n: Spontaneity itself: the second line simply repeats "one cup" three times. The third line borrows from Tao Yuanming, who used to tell his guests "I'm drunk and want to sleep — you may go" — the frankness of true friends.

poems.s: night moon clouds pine tower
z: 小时不识月，呼作白玉盘。
又疑瑶台镜，飞在青云端。
e: When I was small, I didn't know the moon —
I called it a white jade plate up in the sky,
Or thought it was the Jasper Terrace mirror,
Flying above the blue clouds, way up high.
poems.n: The opening of a longer poem, recited by every Chinese child: a little boy's guesses at what the moon must be. The Jasper Terrace (瑶台) is the dwelling of immortals, so the moon is their mirror.

poems.s: autumn river butterfly cottage maple person
z: 妾发初覆额，折花门前剧。
郎骑竹马来，绕床弄青梅。
同居长干里，两小无嫌猜。
十四为君妇，羞颜未尝开。
低头向暗壁，千唤不一回。
十五始展眉，愿同尘与灰。
常存抱柱信，岂上望夫台。
十六君远行，瞿塘滟滪堆。
五月不可触，猿声天上哀。
门前迟行迹，一一生绿苔。
苔深不能扫，落叶秋风早。
八月蝴蝶黄，双飞西园草。
感此伤妾心，坐愁红颜老。
早晚下三巴，预将书报家。
相迎不道远，直至长风沙。
e: When my hair was cut in bangs above my brow,
I played by the gate, picking flowers in the sun;
You came riding on your bamboo horse, and how
We circled the well-rail, tossing green plums, just for fun.
We lived together in the lane of Changgan,
Two little ones, without suspicion or care.
At fourteen I became your wife, my man —
So shy I never smiled, I'd hardly dare;
I hung my head and faced the shadowed wall;
A thousand times you called — I never turned at all.
At fifteen my brows unknit; I wished to be
With you as dust and ashes, endlessly.
I kept the faith of the man who held the pillar fast —
Why would I climb the Watching-for-Husband Tower at last?
At sixteen you went far away from me,
Past Qutang Gorge, where Yanyu's rocks rear high —
In the fifth month, no boat can touch them safely,
And the gibbons wail up in the sky.
Before the gate, the footprints that you left behind
Have each grown over, one by one, with moss of green;
The moss is deep, too deep to sweep, I find;
Leaves fall early in the autumn wind, I've seen.
In the eighth month, yellow butterflies,
In pairs, fly over the west garden's grass;
It wounds my heart to see them; my youth flies,
And I sit grieving as my looks fade and pass.
Sooner or later, when you come down from the Three Ba,
Send me a letter home ahead — I'll go and wait;
I won't say it's far: I'll come to meet you,
All the way to Long Wind Sands, beyond the gate.
poems.n: A young merchant's wife writes to her husband trading far up the Yangtze. Her childhood with him gave Chinese two idioms for childhood sweethearts — 青梅竹马 "green plums and bamboo horse" and 两小无猜 "two little ones without suspicion". The "man who held the pillar" waited for his love under a bridge until the flood drowned him; the Watching-for-Husband Tower is where wives waited in vain. Ezra Pound's free version, *The River-Merchant's Wife: A Letter*, is one of the most famous translations in English.

poems.s: spring palace flowers clouds mist
z: 一枝红艳露凝香，云雨巫山枉断肠。
借问汉宫谁得似，可怜飞燕倚新妆。
e: A spray of crimson glory, fragrance gathered in the dew —
The goddess of Wu's cloud and rain broke hearts, but all in vain.
Who in the Han palace could have matched her? Tell me, who?
Sweet Flying Swallow, maybe — after making up again.
poems.n: The second of the three peony songs for Consort Yang. The goddess of Mount Wu, who visited a king "as cloud at dawn and rain at dusk", is no match for her; only Zhao Feiyan ("Flying Swallow"), the Han emperor's slender favourite, comes close — and only after doing her make-up. Later enemies claimed the comparison was a veiled insult, since Feiyan was notorious; it may have helped get Li Bai sent away from court.

poems.s: spring palace flowers pavilion
z: 名花倾国两相欢，长得君王带笑看。
解释春风无限恨，沉香亭北倚阑干。
e: The famous flower and the beauty who could topple states delight each other so,
And win the sovereign's smiling gaze forever, as they stand.
They melt away the endless sorrows that the spring winds blow —
North of the Aloeswood Pavilion, leaning on the rail, hand in hand.
poems.n: The last of the peony songs: flower and woman are now one pair, both 倾国 — beauty that "topples a kingdom", a phrase from a Han song. Leaning on the balustrade of the Aloeswood Pavilion, they dispel all of spring's melancholy. Within a dozen years the An Lushan rebellion would topple the kingdom in earnest, and Consort Yang would be put to death.

poems.s: night autumn moon leaves crows
z: 秋风清，秋月明，
落叶聚还散，寒鸦栖复惊。
相思相见知何日？此时此夜难为情！
入我相思门，知我相思苦，
长相思兮长相忆，短相思兮无穷极。
早知如此绊人心，何如当初莫相识。
e: Autumn wind clear,
Autumn moon bright;
Fallen leaves gather, then scatter in flight;
Cold crows settle, then start up in fright.
When shall we, who long for each other, meet? Who knows?
This hour, this night, how hard to bear these woes!
Once you have entered love's gate,
You know how bitter longing can be:
Long longing — long remembering;
Short longing — no end that I see.
Had I known how it would bind my heart so,
Better we'd never met, long ago.
poems.n: Called the "three-five-seven-character poem" for its lines that grow from three to five to seven characters, like a rising breath. The leaves that gather and scatter, the crows that settle and are startled, mirror the restless heart. The famous last couplet — "had I known it would bind my heart like this, better we had never met" — is still quoted by lovers today.

poems.s: spring pavilion willow wind two
z: 天下伤心处，劳劳送客亭。
春风知别苦，不遣柳条青。
e: Of all the places under heaven where hearts break,
None like Laolao Pavilion, where travellers are sent.
The spring wind knows how bitter partings make —
It will not let the willows green, for that's what partings meant.
poems.n: Laolao Pavilion, south of Nanjing, was the traditional place to see travellers off. Because parting friends broke off willow twigs as keepsakes, the poet imagines the spring wind kindly holding back the willows' green — no twigs, no partings.

poems.te: Climbing Xie Tiao's North Tower at Xuancheng in Autumn
poems.s: autumn dusk tower river bridge hills mist
z: 江城如画里，山晚望晴空。
两水夹明镜，双桥落彩虹。
人烟寒橘柚，秋色老梧桐。
谁念北楼上，临风怀谢公。
e: The river town lies as if painted in a scroll;
At evening, from the hills, I watch the cloudless sky.
Two streams enclose a mirror, bright and whole;
Twin bridges fall like rainbows from on high.
Chimney smoke chills the oranges and pomelos;
Autumn's colour ages the wutong trees.
Who'd think that here, upon the North Tower, someone knows
And thinks of Lord Xie, facing the breeze?
poems.n: Xuancheng (Anhui), between two rivers, was governed in the 5th century by the poet Xie Tiao, whom Li Bai revered. The middle couplets are among the most painterly in Tang verse — the bridges reflected as rainbows, the cold blue smoke among the fruit trees, autumn "aging" the wutongs. Li Bai, alone at the top, feels a kinship across three centuries.

poems.te: Listening to the Monk Jun of Shu Play the Qin
poems.s: autumn dusk pine mountains temple person clouds
z: 蜀僧抱绿绮，西下峨眉峰。
为我一挥手，如听万壑松。
客心洗流水，余响入霜钟。
不觉碧山暮，秋云暗几重。
e: A monk from Shu, his Green Silk qin in hand,
Came west from the peaks of Emei's height.
He swept his hand across the strings for me —
I heard ten thousand valleys' pines take flight.
My traveller's heart was washed as by a stream;
The echoes merged with frosty temple bells.
I did not notice the green hills grow dark,
Till autumn clouds had dimmed them, swells on swells.
poems.n: The qin (seven-stringed zither) was the scholar's instrument. Green Silk (绿绮) was the name of a famous ancient qin. "Flowing water" recalls the legendary friendship of Boya, who played, and Ziqi, who alone understood him — so the music both cleanses the poet and makes the two men soul-friends. The bell rung in frost was said to resonate of itself.

poems.s: day pine clouds mountains person cottage
z: 吾爱孟夫子，风流天下闻。
红颜弃轩冕，白首卧松云。
醉月频中圣，迷花不事君。
高山安可仰，徒此揖清芬。
e: I love you, Master Meng, my friend —
Your grace and style the whole world knows.
In youth you spurned the carriage and the crown;
Now white-haired, you lie where pine and cloud repose.
Drunk by the moon, you often "hit the sage";
Lost in the flowers, you will serve no king.
A mountain so high — how can I look up to it?
I can only bow to your pure fragrance as I sing.
poems.n: Li Bai's tribute to Meng Haoran, the older poet who never held office. "Hitting the sage" (中圣) was Wei-dynasty slang for getting drunk — "sage" meant clear wine. The last couplet quotes the *Book of Songs*: "the high mountain I look up to" — a phrase for supreme admiration.

poems.te: Mooring at Niuzhu at Night, Thinking of the Past
poems.s: night autumn moon river boat maple leaves
z: 牛渚西江夜，青天无片云。
登舟望秋月，空忆谢将军。
余亦能高咏，斯人不可闻。
明朝挂帆席，枫叶落纷纷。
e: At Niuzhu, on the Western River, night;
Not one cloud flecks the blue sky's face.
I climb the deck to watch the autumn moon,
And think in vain of General Xie's grace.
I, too, can chant my poems loud and high —
But such a man will never hear my song.
Tomorrow I will hoist my mat-sail and go,
While maple leaves fall, scattering along.
poems.n: In the 4th century General Xie Shang, mooring here on a moonlit night, overheard a poor boatman named Yuan Hong chanting his own poems, and was so impressed he made him his protégé. Li Bai moors in the same spot — and no patron comes. The falling maple leaves carry the disappointment.

poems.te: Farewell at a Wine Shop in Jinling
poems.s: spring willow cottage river jar cup two
z: 风吹柳花满店香，吴姬压酒劝客尝。
金陵子弟来相送，欲行不行各尽觞。
请君试问东流水，别意与之谁短长？
e: The wind blows willow-down; the whole shop smells of spring;
A girl of Wu presses the wine and bids the guests to taste.
The young men of Jinling have come to see me off — we cling:
I go, yet don't; and each drains cup on cup in haste.
I ask you, friends, go ask the river flowing east —
Which is longer: its flow, or this parting's feast?
poems.n: Li Bai, about 25, leaving Nanjing for Yangzhou. "Pressing the wine" means straining fresh rice wine from the mash. The image of the endless eastward-flowing river as a measure of feeling became a favourite device of later poets.

poems.te: Holding My Cup, I Ask the Moon
poems.s: night moon clouds sea person cup
z: 青天有月来几时？我今停杯一问之。
人攀明月不可得，月行却与人相随。
皎如飞镜临丹阙，绿烟灭尽清辉发。
但见宵从海上来，宁知晓向云间没。
白兔捣药秋复春，嫦娥孤栖与谁邻？
今人不见古时月，今月曾经照古人。
古人今人若流水，共看明月皆如此。
唯愿当歌对酒时，月光长照金樽里。
e: How long has the moon been in the blue sky? Here,
I put my cup down for a while to ask it so.
Men try to climb up to the moon — it's never near;
Yet as they walk, the moon walks with them where they go.
Bright as a flying mirror over the crimson gate,
When the green mists all have melted, it pours out its clear light.
We see it rising from the sea each night, but late,
Who knows where it sinks among the clouds at dawn's first light?
The white hare pounds its herbs from autumn into spring;
Chang'e lives alone — who is her neighbour there?
People today never saw the ancient moon a-shining,
Yet this moon once shone on the ancients, just as fair.
The ancients and the moderns flow on like a stream,
And all have watched the bright moon, just as we.
I only hope, when I sing over wine, its beam
Will shine into my golden cup eternally.
poems.n: Written at a friend's request. Li Bai muses on the moon's eternity against human transience: the moon follows us yet cannot be reached; it watched the ancients as it watches us. The white hare and the goddess Chang'e are the moon's legendary inhabitants. Su Shi's famous "When will the bright moon appear?" owes much to this poem.

poems.te: Leaving My Children at Nanling for the Capital
poems.s: autumn dusk sun cottage fields person rider
z: 白酒新熟山中归，黄鸡啄黍秋正肥。
呼童烹鸡酌白酒，儿女嬉笑牵人衣。
高歌取醉欲自慰，起舞落日争光辉。
游说万乘苦不早，著鞭跨马涉远道。
会稽愚妇轻买臣，余亦辞家西入秦。
仰天大笑出门去，我辈岂是蓬蒿人。
e: The white wine has just ripened as I come back to the hills;
The yellow hens peck millet, in the autumn fat and fine.
I call the boy to cook a chicken and to pour the wine;
My children laugh and tug my clothes with giggles and with trills.
I sing aloud and drink my fill to soothe my soul;
I rise to dance, and vie in brilliance with the setting sun.
Too late, I've come to counsel the Lord of Ten Thousand Chariots — the goal!
I whip my horse and ride the long road till it's done.
The foolish wife of Kuaiji scorned Zhu Maichen once, they say;
I, too, now leave my home and go west, to Qin, away.
I throw back my head and laugh aloud, and out the gate I stride —
Are men like me to live and die in brambles, cast aside?
poems.n: In 742, aged 41, Li Bai was summoned to court by Emperor Xuanzong. Zhu Maichen was a Han woodcutter whose wife left him for his poverty — and who later rose to high office. The last couplet, a shout of vindication, is one of the most quoted lines Li Bai wrote. (The court career lasted less than two years.)

poems.s: day clouds sea wind birds
z: 大鹏一日同风起，扶摇直上九万里。
假令风歇时下来，犹能簸却沧溟水。
世人见我恒殊调，闻余大言皆冷笑。
宣父犹能畏后生，丈夫未可轻年少。
e: The great Peng bird, one day, will rise up with the wind,
And spiral straight ninety thousand li into the sky;
And even if the wind should drop, and it come down,
It still could toss the waters of the vast sea high.
The people of the world find all my tunes odd,
And when they hear my boasts they sneer and scoff;
But Confucius said the young deserve respect —
A real man shouldn't brush a young man off.
poems.n: Written by the young Li Bai to Li Yong, a famous senior official who had treated him dismissively. The Peng is the colossal bird in *Zhuangzi* that rises ninety thousand li on a whirlwind. Confucius had said "the young are to be held in awe" — so Li Bai turns the sage's words against his elder.

poems.t: 下终南山过斛斯山人宿置酒
poems.te: Coming Down Zhongnan Mountain, I Stay with the Recluse Husi, Who Sets Out Wine
poems.s: dusk moon mountains bamboo cottage two pine
z: 暮从碧山下，山月随人归。
却顾所来径，苍苍横翠微。
相携及田家，童稚开荆扉。
绿竹入幽径，青萝拂行衣。
欢言得所憩，美酒聊共挥。
长歌吟松风，曲尽河星稀。
我醉君复乐，陶然共忘机。
e: At dusk I came down from the jade-green hill;
The mountain moon came home with me.
Looking back on the path I'd come along,
I saw blue haze across the green slopes lie, so free.
Hand in hand, we came to his farmhouse;
The children opened up the thorn-wood gate.
Green bamboo lined the hidden path,
Green vines brushed my clothes as I walked straight.
We talked and laughed, so glad to rest,
And shared the fine wine, cup by cup.
We sang long songs to the wind in the pines,
Till the songs were done, and few stars still were up.
I was drunk, and you were merry too —
Content, we both forgot the world's deceit and its ado.
poems.n: A pastoral evening in the manner of Tao Yuanming. Zhongnan Mountain, south of Chang'an, was home to many hermits. 忘机 — "forgetting scheming" — is the Daoist ideal of a mind free of calculation: a man who has forgotten scheming, the story goes, can play among the seagulls without frightening them.

poems.s: night moon sea clouds sail
z: 日本晁卿辞帝都，征帆一片绕蓬壶。
明月不归沉碧海，白云愁色满苍梧。
e: Lord Chao of Japan has left the imperial capital;
His single sail went circling round the Isles of Penglai.
The bright moon has not returned — it sank beneath the blue sea;
White clouds of sorrow fill the Cangwu sky.
poems.n: Chao Heng was Abe no Nakamaro, a Japanese scholar who passed the Tang examinations and served at court for decades, a friend of Li Bai and Wang Wei. In 753 he set sail for Japan and was reported drowned. In fact he was shipwrecked on the coast of Vietnam and made his way back to Chang'an — but the poem, written in grief, stayed. He is the "bright moon" lost at sea.

poems.s: spring window grass willow wind
z: 燕草如碧丝，秦桑低绿枝。
当君怀归日，是妾断肠时。
春风不相识，何事入罗帏？
e: In Yan, the grass is like fine jade-green thread;
In Qin, the mulberry bows its green boughs low.
The day you long for home at last, I dread,
Will be the day my heart breaks — long ago.
Spring wind, you are a stranger here to me —
Why do you slip into my silken bed-curtains so?
poems.n: A wife in Qin (around Chang'an) thinks of her husband in Yan (the far north-east). Spring comes late in Yan: when his grass is only just sprouting, her mulberries are already heavy — her heart has been breaking for a long time. The last couplet's prim rebuke to the spring wind is a declaration of fidelity.

poems.s: snow mountains fort flag rider
z: 五月天山雪，无花只有寒。
笛中闻折柳，春色未曾看。
晓战随金鼓，宵眠抱玉鞍。
愿将腰下剑，直为斩楼兰。
e: In the fifth month there's still snow on the Tianshan peaks:
No flowers bloom; there's nothing here but cold.
Only in the flute's "Breaking Willows" spring still speaks;
The spring itself, no eye here can behold.
At dawn we fight, to the gongs' and war-drums' beat;
At night we sleep with jade saddles in our arms.
I only wish the sword here at my waist
Could cut down Loulan's king and end these harms.
poems.n: The Tianshan range in Central Asia, where even midsummer is winter. The soldiers know spring only from the tune "Breaking Willows" played on a flute. In 77 BC the Han envoy Fu Jiezi assassinated the treacherous king of Loulan, a desert oasis kingdom; "beheading Loulan" became the soldier's dream of decisive victory.

poems.te: Viewing the Past at Gusu Terrace
poems.s: night moon willow palace lake
z: 旧苑荒台杨柳新，菱歌清唱不胜春。
只今惟有西江月，曾照吴王宫里人。
e: Old parks, a ruined terrace — yet the willows are new;
The water-chestnut songs ring clear, too full of spring to bear.
Now only the moon above the Western River, true,
Once shone on the ladies of the King of Wu's palace there.
poems.n: Gusu Terrace in Suzhou was built by Fuchai, King of Wu, for the legendary beauty Xi Shi, before his kingdom fell to Yue. The new willows and the girls' songs make the ruin unbearable; the moon is the only witness left from those days. Companion piece to *Viewing the Past at Yue*.

poems.s: night autumn moon window clouds candle
z: 长相思，在长安。
络纬秋啼金井阑，微霜凄凄簟色寒。
孤灯不明思欲绝，卷帷望月空长叹。
美人如花隔云端！
上有青冥之高天，下有渌水之波澜。
天长路远魂飞苦，梦魂不到关山难。
长相思，摧心肝！
e: Endless longing —
In Chang'an town.
The crickets cry in autumn by the golden well-rail's crown;
A light frost, chill and bleak; my bamboo mat is cold.
My lonely lamp burns dim; my longing's near to death;
I roll the curtain, watch the moon, and sigh with empty breath.
My love, like a flower, is far beyond the clouds!
Above, the blue and boundless height of heaven;
Below, the clear and rippling waves.
The sky is wide, the road is long; my soul's flight is hard;
Even in dreams my spirit can't cross the mountain passes barred.
Endless longing —
It breaks my heart!
poems.n: An old ballad title. The beloved "like a flower beyond the clouds" may be a woman — or, in a long tradition of Chinese allegory, the emperor whom the exiled poet longs to serve. Either reading makes the soul that cannot even reach its goal in dreams heartbreaking.

poems.te: Seeing a Friend Off to Shu
poems.s: spring peaks clouds rider river wall
z: 见说蚕丛路，崎岖不易行。
山从人面起，云傍马头生。
芳树笼秦栈，春流绕蜀城。
升沉应已定，不必问君平。
e: They say the road to Cancong's land of Shu
Is steep and rough, and hard to travel through:
Mountains rise right up before your face;
Clouds are born beside your horse's head.
Yet fragrant trees will shade the plank roads of Qin,
And spring streams circle Shu's walled town, instead.
Your rise or fall in life is fixed already —
No need to ask Junping to have it read.
poems.n: Gentler than *The Road to Shu Is Hard*: the dizzying middle lines — mountains rising from in front of your face, clouds born beside the horse's head — give way to spring trees and streams. Yan Junping was a famous Han fortune-teller of Chengdu. Li Bai, recently out of favour himself, offers a friend philosophical calm.

poems.te: Staying with Old Mother Xun Below Five Pines Mountain
poems.s: night autumn moon cottage pine fields
z: 我宿五松下，寂寥无所欢。
田家秋作苦，邻女夜舂寒。
跪进雕胡饭，月光明素盘。
令人惭漂母，三谢不能餐。
e: I stayed the night beneath Five Pines,
So lonely, with no pleasure there to find.
Farm folk toil bitterly in autumn;
Next door, girls pound grain in the cold at night.
She knelt to offer me wild-rice dinner —
The moonlight lit the plain white plate.
I felt ashamed, as before the washer-woman,
And thanked her thrice, but could not eat.
poems.n: A rare glimpse of Li Bai humbled. A poor old farm woman serves him precious wild rice (雕胡, the grain of *Zizania*). The washer-woman (漂母) fed the starving young Han Xin, later a great general, who rewarded her with a thousand gold; Li Bai knows he can never repay such kindness.

poems.s: night moon petals river person birds
z: 对酒不觉暝，落花盈我衣。
醉起步溪月，鸟还人亦稀。
e: Drinking, I didn't notice dusk come on;
Fallen blossoms filled the folds of my gown.
Drunk, I rise and walk along the moonlit stream;
The birds are home; few people are around.
poems.n: Twenty characters of pure contentment. Time slips by unnoticed, petals pile up on his clothes, and he wanders tipsily by a stream full of moonlight as the world goes quiet.

poems.s: spring sun flowers hills
z: 红豆生南国，春来发几枝。
愿君多采撷，此物最相思。
e: Red beans grow in the southern land;
When spring comes, how many sprigs appear?
I hope you'll gather many in your hand —
They hold the deepest longing, dear.
poems.n: The red bean (红豆), a bright scarlet seed of the south, is called the "love-longing seed" (相思子) after a legend of a woman who wept beneath a tree for her husband killed at the frontier until her tears turned into red beans. Wang Wei wrote the poem for his friend, the singer Li Guinian, who sang it at banquets; it became one of the most-sung lyrics of the Tang.

poems.s: dusk mountains pine sun mist
z: 空山不见人，但闻人语响。
返景入深林，复照青苔上。
e: On the empty mountain, no one can be seen —
Yet voices echo, somewhere, faintly heard.
The sunset's light comes back into the deep woods,
And shines again upon the moss of green.
poems.n: One of the twenty quatrains of the *Wangchuan Collection*, written at Wang Wei's country estate. Nothing happens — voices without people, a slant of evening light on moss — yet the poem has been called the purest expression of Chan (Zen) stillness in Chinese verse. Translators love it: Eliot Weinberger wrote a whole book, *Nineteen Ways of Looking at Wang Wei*, comparing versions of these twenty characters.

poems.s: night moon bamboo person
z: 独坐幽篁里，弹琴复长啸。
深林人不知，明月来相照。
e: Alone I sit among the dark bamboo,
I pluck my zither, then I whistle long.
Deep in the woods, where no one knows I'm here,
The bright moon comes to shine upon my song.
poems.n: Another Wangchuan poem. "Long whistling" (长啸) was a Daoist breathing art and a free spirit's way of expressing feeling. No one hears the music — except the moon, which comes as a friend.

poems.s: night spring moon mountains petals birds
z: 人闲桂花落，夜静春山空。
月出惊山鸟，时鸣春涧中。
e: At ease, I hear the cassia blossoms fall;
The night is still; the spring hills empty lie.
The rising moon startles the mountain birds —
From time to time, they in the spring ravine cry.
poems.n: So quiet that one can hear tiny flowers dropping; so still that moonrise startles the birds. Sound is used to deepen silence — a classic technique of Chinese verse. (桂花 here is probably a spring-flowering cassia or osmanthus.)

poems.s: dusk autumn moon pine mountains river bamboo lotus boat
z: 空山新雨后，天气晚来秋。
明月松间照，清泉石上流。
竹喧归浣女，莲动下渔舟。
随意春芳歇，王孙自可留。
e: In the empty hills, after fresh rain,
The evening air brings autumn on.
The bright moon shines among the pines;
Clear spring water over stones runs on.
Bamboos rustle — washing girls come home;
Lotus leaves stir — down go fishing boats.
Let spring's fragrance fade as it will:
Here a prince may stay, content to remain.
poems.n: Wang Wei's best-loved regulated poem. The famous second couplet — moon among pines, water over stones — is a perfect ink painting. An old song called on "princes" (gentlemen) to leave the wild mountains, since "spring grasses grow, and you cannot stay"; Wang Wei turns it around: the hills, even in autumn, are where one belongs.

poems.te: Seeing Off Yuan the Second on His Mission to Anxi
poems.s: dawn spring rain willow cottage cup two
z: 渭城朝雨浥轻尘，客舍青青柳色新。
劝君更尽一杯酒，西出阳关无故人。
e: The morning rain in Weicheng lays the light dust low;
Around the inn, the willows' fresh green glows.
Come, drink one more cup of wine before you go —
West of Yang Pass, there's no old friend who knows.
poems.n: Anxi was the Tang protectorate in Central Asia; Yang Pass, near Dunhuang, was the last gate of China. This quatrain was set to music as the *Three Refrains at Yang Pass* (阳关三叠), the most famous farewell song in Chinese history, sung at partings for a thousand years. The willows, as always, are a parting gift.

poems.te: Thinking of My Brothers in Shandong on the Double Ninth
poems.s: autumn mountains chrysanthemum person
z: 独在异乡为异客，每逢佳节倍思亲。
遥知兄弟登高处，遍插茱萸少一人。
e: Alone, a stranger in a stranger's land,
At every festival I miss my family twice as much.
Far off, I know my brothers climb the heights,
Each wearing dogwood — all but one, out of touch.
poems.n: Written when Wang Wei was only seventeen, living in the capital. On the Double Ninth (the 9th day of the 9th month), families climbed hills and wore sprigs of cornel (茱萸) to ward off evil. Instead of saying "I miss them", he imagines them missing him. Line two is the proverb every Chinese person far from home quotes at festival time.

poems.s: dusk sun desert smoke river geese rider
z: 单车欲问边，属国过居延。
征蓬出汉塞，归雁入胡天。
大漠孤烟直，长河落日圆。
萧关逢候骑，都护在燕然。
e: With a single carriage I go to visit the frontier,
Past Juyan and the vassal lands beyond.
Like tumbleweed blown out of the Han passes,
Like a wild goose winging home into the Hu sky.
Across the vast desert, a lone smoke rising straight;
Above the long river, the setting sun hangs round.
At Xiao Pass I meet a mounted scout:
"The Protector-General is at Mount Yanran."
poems.n: 737: Wang Wei was sent as an envoy to congratulate a general on a victory in the north-west. The third couplet — a single plume of beacon smoke dead straight in the windless desert, the sun perfectly round over the Yellow River — was praised in *Dream of the Red Chamber* as the ideal of a line that is "unreasonable, yet more true than reason". Mount Yanran was where a Han general carved a record of his victory over the Xiongnu.

poems.s: winter plum window snow
z: 君自故乡来，应知故乡事。
来日绮窗前，寒梅著花未？
e: You've just come from our old hometown —
You must know how things there are going.
The day you left, before my latticed window,
Had the winter plum begun its blossoming?
poems.n: Of all the things he could ask about home — family, friends, the harvest — the poet asks only about one plum tree outside his window. The smallest detail carries the whole of homesickness.

poems.s: dusk spring mountains cottage grass
z: 山中相送罢，日暮掩柴扉。
春草明年绿，王孙归不归？
e: In the hills, I've seen my friend off on his way;
At dusk I close my rough brushwood gate.
When spring grass turns green again next year,
Will you come back, my prince, or will I wait?
poems.n: The farewell is already over in the first line; the poem lives in the moment after — the gate closed in the dusk, and a question thrown forward to next spring. "Spring grass and the wandering prince" echoes the *Songs of Chu*: "The prince wanders and does not return; spring grass grows thick."

poems.s: day mountains clouds rider two cup
z: 下马饮君酒，问君何所之？
君言不得意，归卧南山陲。
但去莫复问，白云无尽时。
e: Dismount and drink this wine with me —
Where are you going, may I ask?
You say the world has not gone well for you;
You'll lie down by the Southern Mountains, leave your task.
Then go — I'll ask no more:
White clouds are endless, as before.
poems.n: A friend gives up his career to become a recluse. Wang Wei does not argue or console; the white clouds — symbol of the free, unworldly life — are "without end", unlike fame and office. The restraint is the comfort.

poems.s: day mountains clouds river person pine
z: 中岁颇好道，晚家南山陲。
兴来每独往，胜事空自知。
行到水穷处，坐看云起时。
偶然值林叟，谈笑无还期。
e: In middle age I came to love the Way;
In later years I made my home where the South Hills end.
When the mood comes, I often go alone;
Its joys are mine to know, and no one else's, friend.
I walk to where the stream runs out,
And sit to watch the clouds begin to rise.
By chance I meet an old man of the woods;
We talk and laugh, and lose track of the time that flies.
poems.n: "Walk to where the water ends, sit and watch the clouds rise" (行到水穷处，坐看云起时) is one of the most quoted couplets in Chinese — a Zen image of following life wherever it goes: where one path ends, another begins in the sky.

poems.s: day river mountains boat mist wall
z: 楚塞三湘接，荆门九派通。
江流天地外，山色有无中。
郡邑浮前浦，波澜动远空。
襄阳好风日，留醉与山翁。
e: Here Chu's frontier joins the three Xiang rivers;
At Jingmen, nine branches of the River meet.
The river flows beyond heaven and earth;
The hills' hues hover between being and not being.
Towns and cities float on the shore ahead;
The waves set the far sky trembling, shaking free.
Xiangyang has such fine wind and sun —
Let me stay drunk here, like the Old Mountain Man, with glee.
poems.n: Wang Wei was a painter as much as a poet, and line four — mountains "between existence and non-existence" — is a description of ink-wash painting itself, where distant hills dissolve into blank silk. The Old Mountain Man was Shan Jian, a Jin-dynasty governor of Xiangyang famous for getting drunk at its scenic pools.

poems.s: winter wind rider horse fields clouds birds
z: 风劲角弓鸣，将军猎渭城。
草枯鹰眼疾，雪尽马蹄轻。
忽过新丰市，还归细柳营。
回看射雕处，千里暮云平。
e: The wind is strong; the horn-bows twang —
The general hunts by Weicheng town.
The grass is withered; sharp are the falcons' eyes;
The snow is gone; the horses' hooves fly light.
Suddenly they're past the Xinfeng market,
And back again at Willow Camp tonight.
He turns to look where he shot down the eagle:
A thousand li of evening clouds lie flat and bright.
poems.n: Admired for its opening — the sound of the bows comes before we even see the general — and its sweeping close. Willow Camp (细柳营) was the camp of the famously disciplined Han general Zhou Yafu; "shooting the eagle" (射雕) was the mark of a supreme archer.

poems.s: spring mountains flowers petals river
z: 木末芙蓉花，山中发红萼。
涧户寂无人，纷纷开且落。
e: On the tips of the branches, lotus-like blooms
Put out their red buds in the hills.
By the stream-side huts, silent, no one —
They open, and then fall, in flurries, still.
poems.n: From the *Wangchuan Collection*. The magnolia (辛夷) blooms high on bare branches like lotus flowers. No one sees them; they open and fall, entirely for themselves. A Buddhist image of things arising and passing away, without purpose or witness.

poems.s: dusk sun fields cottage person birds
z: 斜光照墟落，穷巷牛羊归。
野老念牧童，倚杖候荆扉。
雉雊麦苗秀，蚕眠桑叶稀。
田夫荷锄至，相见语依依。
即此羡闲逸，怅然吟式微。
e: The slanting light falls on the village;
Down the lanes the cattle and sheep come home.
An old man, thinking of the herd-boy,
Leans on his staff and waits by the thorn-wood gate.
Pheasants call; the wheat is in the ear;
Silkworms sleep; the mulberry leaves grow thin.
Farmers come back with hoes on their shoulders;
They meet and chat, reluctant to part.
It's this I envy — such leisure and ease;
Wistfully I chant, "Why not go home?"
poems.n: A gentle evening of farm life, envied by an official tired of the court. "Why not go home" (式微) is the refrain of a *Book of Songs* poem urging a return home — here, to a simple life.

poems.te: Written at Wangchuan Villa after Long Rain
poems.s: summer rain fields crane oriole cottage smoke pine
z: 积雨空林烟火迟，蒸藜炊黍饷东菑。
漠漠水田飞白鹭，阴阴夏木啭黄鹂。
山中习静观朝槿，松下清斋折露葵。
野老与人争席罢，海鸥何事更相疑。
e: After long rain, in the empty woods, the cooking smoke climbs slow;
Steamed greens and millet go out to the eastern fields below.
Across the misty paddies, white egrets glide;
In the shady summer trees, golden orioles sing.
In the hills I practise stillness, watching morning glories close;
Under the pines, I keep a pure fast, picking dewy mallows' green.
This old rustic no longer jostles others for a seat —
Why should the seagulls still suspect what I mean?
poems.n: Wang Wei, a devout Buddhist, at his country villa. The middle couplets are famous for their painterly colours. The ending alludes to two Daoist stories: a man who gave up his airs found strangers no longer deferred to him at inns; and a man without guile could play with seagulls — until the day he meant to catch one, and they flew away.

poems.s: winter mountains river maple mist
z: 荆溪白石出，天寒红叶稀。
山路元无雨，空翠湿人衣。
