e: White stones jut out in the Jing Creek;
The weather's cold; red leaves are few.
Along the mountain path there was no rain —
Yet the empty green dampens my clothes through.
poems.n: The last two lines are a famous paradox: no rain fell, but the mountain greenery is so dense and moist that it seems to soak the walker. Su Shi said of Wang Wei, "in his poems there are paintings" — with this poem as an example.

poems.s: night moon pine person river fisher
z: 晚年惟好静，万事不关心。
自顾无长策，空知返旧林。
松风吹解带，山月照弹琴。
君问穷通理，渔歌入浦深。
e: In my late years I care for stillness only;
The world's ten thousand things are not my care.
I look at myself: I have no grand designs,
Just the knowledge to go back to my old forest there.
The pine wind blows my loosened belt;
The mountain moon lights me as I play.
You ask me the truth of failure and success? —
A fisherman's song drifts deep into the bay.
poems.n: A friend asked Wang Wei about the principles of worldly success and failure. His answer is no answer: a fisherman's song fading into the reeds. In the *Songs of Chu*, a fisherman sang to Qu Yuan of adapting to the times — but Wang Wei just lets the song drift away.

poems.te: Visiting the Temple of Gathered Fragrance
poems.s: dusk mountains pine temple clouds lake
z: 不知香积寺，数里入云峰。
古木无人径，深山何处钟。
泉声咽危石，日色冷青松。
薄暮空潭曲，安禅制毒龙。
e: I did not know the Temple of Gathered Fragrance;
For miles I climbed into the cloudy peaks.
Ancient trees, no path for human feet;
Deep in the hills, a bell — from where it speaks?
The spring's voice chokes among the jagged rocks;
The sunlight chills upon the green pines' crown.
At dusk, beside the bend of an empty pool,
Calm meditation tames the poison dragon down.
poems.n: The temple is never reached in the poem — only sensed, through a bell and the stillness. The famous fifth and sixth lines turn sound into a sob and light into cold. The "poison dragon" is a Buddhist image of the passions, subdued by meditation.

poems.s: day peaks clouds mist river person
z: 太乙近天都，连山到海隅。
白云回望合，青霭入看无。
分野中峰变，阴晴众壑殊。
欲投人处宿，隔水问樵夫。
e: Taiyi soars close to heaven's capital;
Range on range, it runs to the sea's far end.
White clouds close behind me as I look back;
Blue haze vanishes as I step in.
The central peak divides the starry fields;
Sun and shade are different in each ravine.
Wanting a place where people live, to spend the night,
I call across the stream to a woodcutter, seen.
poems.n: Zhongnan (also called Taiyi), south of Chang'an, is so huge that its central peak was said to divide two astrological zones. The second couplet captures the experience of walking into mist: clouds close up behind, haze dissolves ahead. A single tiny woodcutter at the end gives the scale.

poems.s: spring tower willow horse rider
z: 新丰美酒斗十千，咸阳游侠多少年。
相逢意气为君饮，系马高楼垂柳边。
e: Xinfeng's fine wine costs ten thousand a jug;
Xianyang's gallant knights are mostly young.
When they meet and hearts take fire, they drink to each other,
Their horses tied by the high tower where the willows hung.
poems.n: A dashing glimpse of the young knights-errant of the capital: fine wine, instant friendship, horses tethered beneath the willows of a wine tower. Written when Wang Wei himself was young.

poems.s: spring mountains waterfall flowers birds
z: 远看山有色，近听水无声。
春去花还在，人来鸟不惊。
e: From afar, the mountains have their colours;
Close up, the water makes no sound.
Spring has gone, yet the flowers remain;
People come, yet the birds don't flutter round.
poems.n: A riddle-poem that every Chinese child learns: what landscape has silent water, flowers that never fade, and birds that never fly away? A painting. The attribution to Wang Wei is traditional but uncertain.

poems.te: Seeing Shen Zifu Off to Jiangdong
poems.s: spring willow river boat two
z: 杨柳渡头行客稀，罟师荡桨向临圻。
惟有相思似春色，江南江北送君归。
e: At the willow ferry, few travellers remain;
The boatman rows his oars toward Linqi's shore.
Only my longing, like the colours of spring,
Will follow you home, south and north of the River, evermore.
poems.n: The final image is lovely: spring is everywhere on both banks of the Yangtze, and so is the poet's affection, accompanying his friend all the way home.

poems.s: day rain cottage grass window
z: 轻阴阁小雨，深院昼慵开。
坐看苍苔色，欲上人衣来。
e: Light clouds hold back the drizzle;
The deep courtyard gate, at noon, I'm too lazy to undo.
I sit and gaze at the green of the moss —
It seems about to climb onto my clothes, too.
poems.n: A drowsy moment after rain. The moss is so vividly green that, in the stillness, it seems ready to creep up onto the watcher — the boundary between self and world dissolving.

poems.s: dusk autumn sun mountains river birds wall rider
z: 清川带长薄，车马去闲闲。
流水如有意，暮禽相与还。
荒城临古渡，落日满秋山。
迢递嵩高下，归来且闭关。
e: A clear stream girds the long thickets;
My carriage moves at an easy pace.
The flowing water seems to have a will;
The evening birds fly home with me apace.
A ruined city by an ancient ferry;
The setting sun fills the autumn hills.
Far off, below the heights of Mount Song,
I'll come home and shut my gate, and keep still.
poems.n: A journey home into retirement. The water and the homing birds seem to share his mood; the ruined city and sunset bring a touch of melancholy before the final resolution — to close the gate on the world.

poems.s: dawn spring peach willow mist cottage oriole
z: 桃红复含宿雨，柳绿更带朝烟。
花落家童未扫，莺啼山客犹眠。
e: Pink peach blossoms still hold last night's rain;
Green willows wear the morning's misty veil.
Fallen flowers — the houseboy hasn't swept them;
Orioles sing — the mountain guest still sleeps, all hale.
poems.n: A rare six-character quatrain, every line packed with colour and parallelism. Nothing needs doing: the petals can lie, the guest can sleep.

poems.s: spring palace flowers window
z: 莫以今时宠，能忘旧日恩。
看花满眼泪，不共楚王言。
e: Don't think that the favour she's shown today
Could make her forget the love of before.
She gazes at flowers, her eyes full of tears,
And will not speak to the King of Chu anymore.
poems.n: In 680 BC the King of Chu destroyed the state of Xi and took its queen for himself. She bore him two sons but, the *Zuo Zhuan* records, never spoke to him. Wang Wei wrote this at a banquet where a prince had taken a pancake-seller's wife; shown her old husband, she wept — and the prince let her go home.

poems.s: winter snow geese clouds sun two rider
z: 千里黄云白日曛，北风吹雁雪纷纷。
莫愁前路无知己，天下谁人不识君。
e: A thousand li of yellow cloud; the white sun's dim and low;
The north wind blows the wild geese on through swirling snow.
Don't fear the road ahead will hold no friend who knows your name —
Who in all the world is there who doesn't know your fame?
poems.n: Dong the Elder was Dong Tinglan, the greatest qin player of the age. Gao Shi, then poor and unknown, sees him off in a snowstorm with no gift but this encouragement — one of the most heartening farewell poems ever written.

poems.s: night winter candle cottage person
z: 旅馆寒灯独不眠，客心何事转凄然。
故乡今夜思千里，霜鬓明朝又一年。
e: At the inn, beside a cold lamp, alone and wide awake —
Why does this traveller's heart turn so forlorn and drear?
Tonight, a thousand li away, my family thinks of me;
By morning, my frost-grey temples will have aged another year.
poems.n: New Year's Eve, the great night of family reunion, spent alone at an inn. Again the turn: it is his family who are thinking of him. At midnight everyone in China grows a year older — his grey hair with them.

poems.te: Hearing a Flute on the Frontier
poems.s: night moon fort mountains horse petals snow
z: 雪净胡天牧马还，月明羌笛戍楼间。
借问梅花何处落，风吹一夜满关山。
e: The snow is gone; beneath the Hu sky, the horse herds come back home;
In bright moonlight a Qiang flute plays among the watchtowers there.
And where, I ask, do the plum blossoms fall?
The wind blows them all night, filling the passes everywhere.
poems.n: A beautiful double image. "Plum Blossoms Falling" (梅花落) was a flute tune; the poet imagines its notes, like petals, blown by the wind over all the mountain passes. Flowers, music and homesickness merge.

poems.s: dusk desert fort flag rider mountains
z: 汉家烟尘在东北，汉将辞家破残贼。
男儿本自重横行，天子非常赐颜色。
𪭢金伐鼓下榆关，旌旆逶迤碣石间。
校尉羽书飞瀚海，单于猎火照狼山。
山川萧条极边土，胡骑凭陵杂风雨。
战士军前半死生，美人帐下犹歌舞。
大漠穷秋塞草腓，孤城落日斗兵稀。
身当恩遇恒轻敌，力尽关山未解围。
铁衣远戍辛勤久，玉箸应啼别离后。
少妇城南欲断肠，征人蓟北空回首。
边庭飘飖那可度，绝域苍茫更何有。
杀气三时作阵云，寒声一夜传刁斗。
相看白刃血纷纷，死节从来岂顾勋。
君不见沙场征战苦，至今犹忆李将军。
e: Smoke and dust of war rise in the Han's north-east;
Han generals leave their homes to crush the rebels, to the least.
Men of spirit prize the chance to ride across the land;
The Son of Heaven grants them favour, rare and grand.
With clanging gongs and pounding drums they march down through Elm Pass;
Their banners wind among the crags of Jieshi, mass on mass.
The colonels' feathered war-reports fly over the desert sea;
On Wolf Mountain the khan's hunting fires blaze free.
Mountains and rivers are desolate to the edge of the frontier ground;
Hu horsemen charge with wind and rain, swarming all around.
At the front, the soldiers — half are dead and half alive;
Beneath the general's tent, the beauties sing and dance and thrive.
In the great desert, autumn's end; the frontier grass is sere;
The lone fort at sunset — few soldiers left to fight are here.
So favoured by the emperor, the general scorned the foe;
Now, strength spent at the passes, the siege won't lift or go.
In iron mail on distant guard through long and bitter years —
Since parting, their wives must weep their jade-chopstick tears.
South of the city, young wives' hearts are breaking with despair;
North in Ji, the soldiers turn their heads in vain, to stare.
The frontier's wild and windswept — how can it be crossed?
The far land's vast and empty — nothing there but loss.
All day the killing-air forms battle clouds on high;
All night the watchmen's gongs ring out their freezing cry.
They face each other's naked blades; the blood in spatters flies —
To die for duty, who would think of honours or of prize?
Have you not seen the bitterness of fighting on the sands?
To this day the soldiers long for General Li to lead their bands.
poems.n: Written in 738 after news of a disastrous campaign in the north-east, where a general's arrogance and false victory reports cost many lives. "At the front, half the soldiers dead; in the general's tent, beauties still singing and dancing" is the most damning couplet in frontier poetry. "Jade chopsticks" are a woman's two streams of tears. General Li is Li Guang of the Han, who shared every hardship with his men.

poems.s: spring wall flowers birds person
z: 国破山河在，城春草木深。
感时花溅泪，恨别鸟惊心。
烽火连三月，家书抵万金。
白头搔更短，浑欲不胜簪。
e: The state lies broken; hills and rivers stay;
Spring in the city: grass and trees grow deep.
Grieved by the times, I see the flowers weep;
Hating our parting, birdsong makes my heart leap.
The beacon fires have burned three months on end;
A letter from home is worth ten thousand gold.
I scratch my white head; the hair grows thinner still —
Soon it will be too thin a pin to hold.
poems.n: Spring 757 in Chang'an, occupied by An Lushan's rebels. Du Fu was trapped in the ruined capital while his family was far away. The first line sets the empire's collapse against the indifferent permanence of nature. Lines 3–4 can be read both ways at once — the flowers and birds weep and start with him, or he weeps and starts at them. A scholar wore his hair in a topknot held with a pin; Du Fu's is falling out from grief.

poems.s: autumn peaks river leaves birds person wind
z: 风急天高猿啸哀，渚清沙白鸟飞回。
无边落木萧萧下，不尽长江滚滚来。
万里悲秋常作客，百年多病独登台。
艰难苦恨繁霜鬓，潦倒新停浊酒杯。
e: The wind is swift, the sky is high, the gibbons cry their grief;
The isle is clear, the sand is white, the birds wheel back around.
Endlessly the falling leaves come rustling, leaf on leaf;
Unendingly the Long River comes rolling on with sound.
Ten thousand li from home, in mournful autumn, a stranger everywhere,
Sick all my life, I climb the terrace alone — no friend of mine.
Hardship and bitter grief have frosted all my hair;
Worn out, I've just given up my cup of cloudy wine.
poems.n: Written in autumn 767 at Kuizhou on the Yangtze, on the Double Ninth Festival, when people climbed heights with their families and drank chrysanthemum wine. Du Fu, fifty-five, sick and far from home, climbs alone — and has had to give up wine for his health. Often called the greatest seven-character regulated poem ever written: every line is part of a parallel pair, and the middle couplet's falling leaves and endless river are an image of time itself.

poems.te: Welcome Rain on a Spring Night
poems.s: night spring rain river boat flowers cottage
z: 好雨知时节，当春乃发生。
随风潜入夜，润物细无声。
野径云俱黑，江船火独明。
晓看红湿处，花重锦官城。
e: Good rain knows its proper season:
It comes in spring, when all things start to grow.
It slips in with the wind by night,
And nourishes the world — so fine, so silent, slow.
The country paths are black with cloud;
A lone boat's lantern on the river is aglow.
At dawn, look where it's red and wet:
Brocade City's flowers hang heavy, row on row.
poems.n: Chengdu, 761, during the happiest years of Du Fu's life, at his thatched cottage. The rain is a considerate friend who "knows" when it is needed and arrives quietly in the night. Brocade City (锦官城) is Chengdu, once the seat of the official in charge of the silk-brocade industry — and in the morning it is indeed brocaded with flowers.

poems.s: spring willow oriole crane mountains snow river sail window
z: 两个黄鹂鸣翠柳，一行白鹭上青天。
窗含西岭千秋雪，门泊东吴万里船。
e: Two golden orioles sing in the emerald willow;
A line of white egrets climbs the blue of the sky.
My window frames the West Range's thousand-autumn snow;
At my gate, boats from Eastern Wu, ten thousand li, lie by.
poems.n: Four lines, four perfectly parallel images — yellow and green, white and blue; near and far; sound and stillness — like four panels of a painted screen. Written at his Chengdu cottage in 764 when peace had briefly returned: the boats from Wu, on the lower Yangtze, mean the river route east is open again.

poems.s: dawn peaks clouds birds mist
z: 岱宗夫如何？齐鲁青未了。
造化钟神秀，阴阳割昏晓。
荡胸生曾云，决眦入归鸟。
会当凌绝顶，一览众山小。
e: What is it like, Mount Tai, the lord of peaks?
Over Qi and Lu its green goes on and on.
Creation gathered here its wonder and its grace;
Its shaded and its sunlit sides divide the dusk and dawn.
Layer on layer the clouds rise, and stir my breast;
Home-flying birds dart into my straining eyes.
One day I'll stand upon its highest crest,
And see how small all other mountains lie.
poems.n: Written by the twenty-four-year-old Du Fu after failing the imperial examination. Mount Tai (岱宗, "the ancestor of mountains") in Shandong, the holiest of China's Five Great Peaks, is so vast that its green spans the old states of Qi and Lu. The last couplet, all youthful ambition, echoes Mencius: "Confucius climbed Mount Tai and found the world small."

poems.te: Meeting Li Guinian South of the River
poems.s: spring petals river two pavilion
z: 岐王宅里寻常见，崔九堂前几度闻。
正是江南好风景，落花时节又逢君。
e: In Prince Qi's mansion I saw you often then;
In Cui the Ninth's great hall I heard you sing.
Now in the south, the scenery's fine again —
And I meet you as the blossoms fall from spring.
poems.n: Li Guinian was the most celebrated singer at Emperor Xuanzong's court in the golden years before the An Lushan rebellion. In 770, the last year of Du Fu's life, the two old men met again as refugees in the south. Nothing sad is said; "the season of falling flowers" says everything about the lost golden age — and about the two of them.

poems.te: Hearing That the Imperial Army Has Recovered Henan and Hebei
poems.s: spring river boat peaks person
z: 剑外忽传收蓟北，初闻涕泪满衣裳。
却看妻子愁何在，漫卷诗书喜欲狂。
白日放歌须纵酒，青春作伴好还乡。
即从巴峡穿巫峡，便下襄阳向洛阳。
e: Beyond Sword Pass, the news has come — the North has been restored!
When first I heard, my tears ran down and drenched my clothes right through.
I look at wife and children — where's their sorrow? Out the door!
I roll my books up, mad with joy — what else is there to do?
In broad daylight I'll sing aloud and drink till I am done;
Spring's green will keep us company — how good to journey home!
Straight from the Gorge of Ba, we'll thread the Gorge of Wu, and run
Down to Xiangyang, and on to Luoyang, never more to roam.
poems.n: Spring 763: after eight years, the An Lushan rebellion was crushed when government troops retook the rebels' base in the north-east (Jibei). Du Fu, a refugee in Sichuan beyond the Sword Gate Pass, hears the news. Called "the most joyful poem of his life", it ends by racing through four place-names, as if the journey home were already happening.

poems.te: Song of My Thatched Hut Torn by the Autumn Wind
poems.s: autumn wind rain cottage bamboo river person
z: 八月秋高风怒号，卷我屋上三重茅。
茅飞渡江洒江郊，高者挂罥长林梢，下者飘转沉塘坳。
南村群童欺我老无力，忍能对面为盗贼。
公然抱茅入竹去，唇焦口燥呼不得，归来倚杖自叹息。
俄顷风定云墨色，秋天漠漠向昏黑。
布衾多年冷似铁，娇儿恶卧踏里裂。
床头屋漏无干处，雨脚如麻未断绝。
自经丧乱少睡眠，长夜沾湿何由彻！
安得广厦千万间，大庇天下寒士俱欢颜，风雨不动安如山。
呜呼！何时眼前突兀见此屋，吾庐独破受冻死亦足！
e: In the eighth month, autumn's high; the wind howls in its rage,
And rolls away three layers of the thatch from off my roof.
The thatch flies over the river, strewn across the farther bank;
The high bits catch and tangle in the treetops of the wood,
The low bits whirl and spin, and sink in hollows of the pond.
The boys of South Village bully me — I'm old and have no strength —
And have the heart to rob me to my face!
They carry off the thatch in broad daylight into the bamboo;
My lips are parched, my mouth is dry, I shout to no avail;
I come back, lean on my stick, and sigh alone.
Soon the wind drops; the clouds turn black as ink;
The autumn sky grows dim and dark toward night.
My cotton quilt, years old, is cold as iron;
My darling boy sleeps badly, and has kicked its lining through.
Above the bed the roof leaks — not a single spot is dry;
The rain falls thick as hemp threads, and never stops.
Since the troubles came I've hardly slept —
Soaked through, how can I last this long night till the light?
Oh, for a mansion of ten thousand rooms and more,
To shelter all the poor scholars under heaven and make them smile,
Unshaken by wind and rain, as steady as a mountain!
Ah! If ever I could see such a house rise up before my eyes,
Then let my hut alone be broken, and I freeze to death — I'd be content!
poems.n: Chengdu, autumn 761. The hut that a year earlier had brought Du Fu such peace is wrecked in a storm. The poem moves from comic misery — the village boys making off with his thatch, his exhausted shouting — to a vast compassion: he would gladly freeze if every poor scholar in the world could have a roof. It is among the most loved expressions of selflessness in Chinese literature.

poems.s: night crescent cottage wall person two
z: 暮投石壕村，有吏夜捉人。
老翁逾墙走，老妇出门看。
吏呼一何怒！妇啼一何苦！
听妇前致词：三男邺城戍。
一男附书至，二男新战死。
存者且偷生，死者长已矣！
室中更无人，惟有乳下孙。
有孙母未去，出入无完裙。
老妪力虽衰，请从吏夜归。
急应河阳役，犹得备晨炊。
夜久语声绝，如闻泣幽咽。
天明登前途，独与老翁别。
e: At dusk I lodged at Shihao village late;
By night an officer came, seizing men.
The old man fled across the wall; his wife went to the gate.
How fierce the officer's shouts! How bitter her crying then!
I heard her come before him and explain:
"My three sons went to guard the city of Ye.
From one of them a letter came again:
Two sons have just been killed in the fray.
The living one scrapes by from day to day;
The dead are gone, forever passed away.
There's no one else inside our home,
But a grandson at his mother's breast;
For him his mother's stayed — but she can't roam:
She hasn't one whole skirt in which she could be dressed.
This old woman's strength is weak, I know,
But let me go with you tonight, I pray:
To answer Heyang's muster, quick, I'll go,
And cook the troops their breakfast at break of day."
Deep in the night the voices died away;
I seemed to hear someone sobbing low.
At dawn I set out on my way,
And only the old man saw me go.
poems.n: Spring 759, after the government army's defeat at Ye, when press-gangs were seizing anyone they could find. Du Fu, lodging in a village in Henan, records without a word of comment: at night the old woman gives herself up to save her family; at dawn only the old man is left to say goodbye. One of the "Three Officers" (三吏), his great war ballads.

poems.te: Thinking of My Brothers on a Moonlit Night
poems.s: night autumn moon geese fort frost
z: 戍鼓断人行，边秋一雁声。
露从今夜白，月是故乡明。
有弟皆分散，无家问死生。
寄书长不达，况乃未休兵。
e: The garrison drums have stopped all travellers on their way;
At the autumn frontier, one wild goose cries in the night.
From tonight on, the dew turns white, as the old seasons say;
The moon, I know, at home is shining far more bright.
I have brothers, but they're scattered far apart;
No home is left to ask if they're alive or dead.
The letters that I send never reach their mark —
And still the wars go on, and still no peace ahead.
poems.n: Qinzhou, autumn 759. The night is "White Dew" (白露), one of the twenty-four solar terms, marking the turn into autumn. A single wild goose — geese fly in families, and stand for brothers — cries alone. "The moon is brighter over my hometown" became a proverb: everything is better at home.

poems.s: night moon stars river boat grass birds
z: 细草微风岸，危樯独夜舟。
星垂平野阔，月涌大江流。
名岂文章著，官应老病休。
飘飘何所似，天地一沙鸥。
e: Fine grass, a gentle breeze along the shore;
A tall mast, and my lonely boat by night.
The stars hang low above the boundless plain;
The moon wells up as the great River takes flight.
Fame — has my writing ever won me that?
Old and sick, I let my office pass me by.
Drifting, drifting — what is it I'm like?
A lone gull between the earth and sky.
poems.n: Written in 765 as Du Fu, having lost his patron in Chengdu, sailed down the Yangtze. The vast, luminous middle couplet — stars sagging to the plain, the moon surging in the current — sets up the final image: one small gull in the immensity of the universe.

poems.s: day lake tower boat clouds person
z: 昔闻洞庭水，今上岳阳楼。
吴楚东南坼，乾坤日夜浮。
亲朋无一字，老病有孤舟。
戎马关山北，凭轩涕泗流。
e: Long had I heard of Dongting's waters wide;
Today I climb the Yueyang Tower's height.
Here Wu and Chu split east and south apart;
Heaven and earth float on it day and night.
From kin and friends, not one word comes to me;
Old and sick, I have one lonely boat.
North of the passes, war-horses still ride —
I lean on the rail and let my tears run free.
poems.n: 768, two years before Du Fu's death. Dongting Lake in Hunan is so vast that the ancient lands of Wu and Chu seem split by it, and the whole universe floats upon it. Against this immensity, Du Fu has nothing — no letters, only a boat, and war still raging in the north.

poems.s: spring pine temple oriole grass
z: 丞相祠堂何处寻？锦官城外柏森森。
映阶碧草自春色，隔叶黄鹂空好音。
三顾频烦天下计，两朝开济老臣心。
出师未捷身先死，长使英雄泪满襟。
e: Where shall I seek the shrine of the great Chancellor of Shu?
Outside Brocade City, where the cypress trees grow tall.
The green grass on the steps makes spring's colour for itself;
Behind the leaves the orioles sing, for no one, after all.
Three visits, urgent, sought his plans to set the world aright;
Two reigns he served, the old minister, with all his heart and might.
He led his army out, but died before the victory —
And ever since, heroes have wept their sleeves wet at the sight.
poems.n: Zhuge Liang (181–234), chancellor of the Shu-Han kingdom in the Three Kingdoms era, is China's model of wisdom and loyalty. Liu Bei visited his thatched hut three times to beg for his counsel; Zhuge Liang served him and then his son, and died in camp in 234 on his fifth northern campaign. Du Fu visited the shrine in Chengdu in 760. The last couplet is quoted whenever a great endeavour is cut short.

poems.te: Remembering Li Bai on a Spring Day
poems.s: spring dusk clouds river willow
z: 白也诗无敌，飘然思不群。
清新庾开府，俊逸鲍参军。
渭北春天树，江东日暮云。
何时一樽酒，重与细论文。
e: Li Bai — your poems have no peer;
Your thoughts float free, far from the crowd's ways:
Fresh and clear as Lord Yu Xin's,
Bold and graceful as Bao Zhao's lays.
North of the Wei, I see spring trees;
East of the River, you watch evening clouds.
When shall we share a jug of wine again,
And talk of poetry, line by line, aloud?
poems.n: Du Fu met Li Bai in 744 and travelled with him; after 745 they never met again. Du Fu wrote some fifteen poems about Li Bai. Yu Xin and Bao Zhao were great poets of the Southern Dynasties. "Spring trees north of the Wei, dusk clouds east of the River" — Du Fu in Chang'an, Li Bai in the south — became a set phrase for friends who miss each other.

poems.s: day clouds river wall flowers
z: 锦城丝管日纷纷，半入江风半入云。
此曲只应天上有，人间能得几回闻。
e: In Brocade City, strings and pipes play every day,
Half on the river wind, half to the clouds they float away.
Such music surely only heaven should possess —
How many times can mortals hear it? Few, I'd say.
poems.n: General Hua Jingding had put down a rebellion in Chengdu, then let his troops loot the city — and, many commentators believe, used music reserved for the emperor at his feasts. Du Fu's lavish praise may be a veiled rebuke: "this belongs in heaven" — that is, at the imperial court, not here.

poems.te: Walking Alone by the River in Search of Flowers (VI)
poems.s: spring flowers peach butterfly oriole cottage
z: 黄四娘家花满蹊，千朵万朵压枝低。
留连戏蝶时时舞，自在娇莺恰恰啼。
e: At Fourth Sister Huang's, the path is filled with flowers;
Thousands of blossoms, myriads, bend the branches low.
The playful butterflies keep dancing, lingering for hours;
The carefree orioles sing their sweet songs, just so.
poems.n: One of seven quatrains Du Fu wrote in Chengdu on a solitary walk in search of spring flowers. Fourth Sister Huang was a neighbour. The doubled sounds 留连, 时时, 自在, 恰恰 make the lines dance and sing like the creatures they describe.

poems.s: spring sun river swallows flowers grass
z: 迟日江山丽，春风花草香。
泥融飞燕子，沙暖睡鸳鸯。
e: Long spring days: the rivers and the hills are fair;
The spring breeze brings the scent of flowers and grass.
The mud has thawed — the swallows fly to build;
On warm sand, mandarin ducks doze as the hours pass.
poems.n: Chengdu, 764. A first poem for many Chinese schoolchildren: four lines, four images of spring — light, scent, motion (swallows gathering soft mud for their nests) and stillness (a pair of mandarin ducks, symbols of devoted couples, asleep on the warm sand).

poems.s: night moon window mist cottage
z: 今夜鄜州月，闺中只独看。
遥怜小儿女，未解忆长安。
香雾云鬟湿，清辉玉臂寒。
何时倚虚幌，双照泪痕干。
e: Tonight the moon shines over Fuzhou far away;
In her chamber, she is watching it alone.
I think with pity of our little ones —
Too young to know I'm in Chang'an, not home.
The scented mist must dampen her cloud-soft hair;
The clear light chills her jade-white arms tonight.
When shall we lean by the thin curtain, side by side,
Our tear-stains dried together in the moonlight?
poems.n: Autumn 756. Du Fu had left his wife and children at Fuzhou to join the new emperor, but was captured by rebels and held in Chang'an. Instead of describing his own longing, he imagines his wife gazing at the moon alone — one of the very few Tang poems about a man's love for his wife, and one of the most tender.

poems.s: spring river cottage flowers birds two jar
z: 舍南舍北皆春水，但见群鸥日日来。
花径不曾缘客扫，蓬门今始为君开。
盘飧市远无兼味，樽酒家贫只旧醅。
肯与邻翁相对饮，隔篱呼取尽余杯。
e: North and south of my house, spring waters everywhere,
And only flocks of gulls come visiting each day.
My flowered path was never swept for any guest;
My wicker gate today, for you, first opens its way.
The market's far — my dinner has no second dish;
My house is poor — the wine's last year's old brew, I fear.
If you'd be willing, let us drink with my old neighbour —
I'll call him over the fence to drain the last cups here.
poems.n: Chengdu, 761: a visit from a county magistrate named Cui. Du Fu's apologies for his humble fare are full of warmth, and the closing picture — calling the old neighbour over the hedge to finish the wine — is the essence of simple country friendship.

poems.s: day river mountains clouds
z: 功盖三分国，名成八阵图。
江流石不转，遗恨失吞吴。
e: His deeds outshone the kingdoms of the three;
The Eight-Array Plan won him undying fame.
The river flows; its stones will never shift —
Regret for the war on Wu is all that still remains.
poems.n: The Eight-Array Plan was Zhuge Liang's battle formation; stone mounds said to mark it stood on a sandbar of the Yangtze at Kuizhou, unmoved by floods for centuries — like his loyalty. The last line has two readings: regret that Liu Bei's disastrous attack on Wu broke their alliance, or regret at never conquering Wu at all.

poems.te: Thinking of Li Bai at the Edge of the Sky
poems.s: autumn wind geese river clouds
z: 凉风起天末，君子意如何？
鸿雁几时到，江湖秋水多。
文章憎命达，魑魅喜人过。
应共冤魂语，投诗赠汨罗。
e: A cool wind rises at the edge of the sky —
My friend, what are your thoughts tonight, I wonder?
When will the wild geese bring your letter by?
The lakes and rivers swell with autumn water.
Fine writing hates a man whose fate goes right;
The goblins gloat when travellers pass their way.
You'll talk, I think, with the wronged ghost tonight,
And cast a poem to him in the Miluo's spray.
poems.n: Qinzhou, 759: Du Fu has heard that Li Bai is being sent into exile in Yelang. "Literature hates a fortunate fate" (文章憎命达) — great writers are doomed to suffer — became proverbial. The "wronged ghost" is Qu Yuan, the slandered poet who drowned himself in the Miluo River, near Li Bai's route into exile. Wild geese were said to carry letters.

poems.s: autumn maple peaks river boat chrysanthemum mist
z: 玉露凋伤枫树林，巫山巫峡气萧森。
江间波浪兼天涌，塞上风云接地阴。
丛菊两开他日泪，孤舟一系故园心。
寒衣处处催刀尺，白帝城高急暮砧。
e: Jade dew has withered and wounded the maple woods;
Wu Mountain and Wu Gorge lie bleak and drear.
On the river, waves leap up to touch the sky;
Over the passes, wind-clouds darken the earth near.
Twice now the chrysanthemums bloom — tears of other days;
My lonely boat stays moored — my heart to my old garden tied.
Everywhere, winter clothes speed knife and ruler on;
High Baidi town, at dusk, hears the pounding mallets outside.
poems.n: The first of "Autumn Meditations", eight linked poems written at Kuizhou in 766 and often considered the summit of Du Fu's art. Autumn in the Three Gorges: the chrysanthemums have bloomed twice since he arrived — two years stranded — and the boat that should take him home stays tied, like his heart. The sound of women beating cloth for winter clothes closes the poem in dusk and cold.

poems.s: dusk mountains desert grass sun
z: 群山万壑赴荆门，生长明妃尚有村。
一去紫台连朔漠，独留青冢向黄昏。
画图省识春风面，环佩空归夜月魂。
千载琵琶作胡语，分明怨恨曲中论。
e: The mountains and ten thousand gorges rush toward Jingmen's gate;
Here's the village where the Bright Consort was born and bred.
Once gone from the Purple Palace to the northern deserts' waste,
She left only a green tomb, facing the dusk ahead.
From a painting, the emperor half-knew her spring-wind face;
Her soul comes home in vain, jade pendants chiming, by moonlight.
For a thousand years the pipa has sung in foreign ways,
And in its melodies her bitter grief is told outright.
poems.n: Wang Zhaojun, the "Bright Consort" (明妃), a Han palace lady, was married off to a Xiongnu khan in 33 BC. Legend says the court painter made her portrait ugly because she refused to bribe him, so the emperor never noticed her until the day she left. Her tomb on the steppe was said to stay green when all the grass around it withered. She became the symbol of talent unrecognised — and of Du Fu himself, far from court.

poems.s: spring tower flowers river clouds mountains
z: 花近高楼伤客心，万方多难此登临。
锦江春色来天地，玉垒浮云变古今。
北极朝廷终不改，西山寇盗莫相侵。
可怜后主还祠庙，日暮聊为梁甫吟。
e: Flowers beside the tower wound a traveller's heart;
In times of trouble everywhere, I climb this height.
Spring on Brocade River fills all heaven and earth;
Clouds on Jade Rampart change, as ages take their flight.
Like the Pole Star, our court will never change;
You bandits of the Western Hills — don't dare invade!
Alas, the Last Lord of Shu still has his temple here;
At dusk I'll chant the Liangfu Song as shadows fade.
poems.n: Chengdu, spring 764. Tibetan armies had briefly taken Chang'an the year before and were raiding Sichuan (the "Western Hills"). Du Fu declares that the Tang court, like the Pole Star, will endure. Liu Shan, the feeble Last Lord of Shu-Han, lost his kingdom yet still has a shrine — a pointed reminder to the reigning emperor. The *Liangfu Song* was a favourite of Zhuge Liang.

poems.s: day bridge wall rider horse flag wind
z: 车辚辚，马萧萧，行人弓箭各在腰。
耶娘妻子走相送，尘埃不见咸阳桥。
牵衣顿足拦道哭，哭声直上干云霄。
道旁过者问行人，行人但云点行频。
或从十五北防河，便至四十西营田。
去时里正与裹头，归来头白还戍边。
边庭流血成海水，武皇开边意未已。
君不闻汉家山东二百州，千村万落生荆杞。
纵有健妇把锄犁，禾生陇亩无东西。
况复秦兵耐苦战，被驱不异犬与鸡。
长者虽有问，役夫敢申恨？
且如今年冬，未休关西卒。
县官急索租，租税从何出？
信知生男恶，反是生女好。
生女犹得嫁比邻，生男埋没随百草。
君不见青海头，古来白骨无人收。
新鬼烦冤旧鬼哭，天阴雨湿声啾啾！
e: The chariots rumble, the horses neigh,
Bows and arrows at each marcher's waist on the way.
Fathers, mothers, wives and children run to see them go;
The dust is so thick that Xianyang Bridge no longer shows.
They clutch at clothes, they stamp, they block the road and cry;
The sound of weeping rises straight up to the sky.
A passer-by beside the road asks one of the men;
The man just says, "They call us up again and again.
Some went north at fifteen to guard the Yellow River's shore;
At forty they were sent out west to farm the army's store.
When they left, the village head bound up their hair;
They came home white — and now they're sent back to the frontier.
At the border, blood has flowed until it formed a sea,
But the Martial Emperor still wants more land — he won't let be.
Have you not heard? In Han's two hundred districts east of the hills,
Ten thousand villages lie choked with thorns that no one tills.
Even where strong wives take the hoe and plough in hand,
The crops grow wild and tangled, every which way, on the land.
And since the men of Qin are tough and can endure the fight,
They're driven out like dogs and chickens, day and night.
Though you, sir, ask me this,
How dare a conscript tell you what's amiss?
Take this winter — even now
They haven't sent the western troops back to the plough.
The county officers press hard for tax that we can't pay —
Where is it to come from? Tell me, sir, I pray.
Truly, it's bad luck to have a son, we've learned;
Far better to have a daughter — the tables have turned.
A girl can still be married to the neighbours next door;
A boy lies buried in the grass, and is seen no more.
Have you not seen, beside the Qinghai Lake,
White bones from ancient times that no one comes to take?
New ghosts rage at their wrongs, and the old ghosts wail;
When skies are dark and the rain is wet, you hear them cry in the gale."
poems.n: About 751, a protest against Emperor Xuanzong's endless wars of conquest. Du Fu disguises the present emperor as "the Martial Emperor" — Emperor Wu of Han — and lets a conscript speak. The reversal of the age-old preference for sons ("a son is buried in the grass") was shocking. Xianyang Bridge crossed the Wei River west of Chang'an, where the troops set out; Qinghai Lake was a killing ground in the wars with Tibet.

poems.s: day fort flag rider mountains
z: 挽弓当挽强，用箭当用长。
射人先射马，擒贼先擒王。
杀人亦有限，列国自有疆。
苟能制侵陵，岂在多杀伤。
e: To draw a bow, then draw a strong one;
To use an arrow, use a long one.
To shoot a man, first shoot his mount;
To catch the bandits, catch their king — that counts.
But killing, too, should have its limit,
And every land has borders — stay within it.
If we can halt the invaders' aggression,
What need for slaughter past all discretion?
poems.n: From a series of nine poems in the voice of a soldier on Xuanzong's campaigns. The first four lines sound like military maxims ("to catch bandits, first catch their king" became a proverb); then the soldier turns: war should be for defence, not conquest.

poems.te: For the Recluse Wei the Eighth
poems.s: night rain cottage candle two jar
z: 人生不相见，动如参与商。
今夕复何夕，共此灯烛光。
少壮能几时，鬓发各已苍。
访旧半为鬼，惊呼热中肠。
焉知二十载，重上君子堂。
昔别君未婚，儿女忽成行。
怡然敬父执，问我来何方。
问答乃未已，驱儿罗酒浆。
夜雨剪春韭，新炊间黄粱。
主称会面难，一举累十觞。
十觞亦不醉，感子故意长。
明日隔山岳，世事两茫茫。
e: In this life, old friends so seldom meet —
Like Shen and Shang, two stars that never share the sky.
What night is this night, then, so sweet,
That we two share this candle's light, you and I?
How long can youth and vigour stay?
Already both our temples have turned grey.
I ask for old friends — half are ghosts by now;
I cry out, and my heart burns, I don't know how.
Who'd think that twenty years would go
Before I climbed into your hall again?
When last we parted, you'd no wife, I know;
Now sons and daughters stand in line — and then
They greet their father's friend with smiling grace
And ask me what far place I've journeyed from.
Before our questions and replies have run their race,
You send them off: "Bring wine, and quickly come!"
Spring chives are cut out in the night rain;
New-cooked rice is mixed with yellow grain.
"It's hard for us to meet," my host declares,
And drinks ten cups to me in one long go;
Ten cups — and still I'm sober: unawares,
Your old affection moves me so.
Tomorrow mountains rise between us two,
And the world's affairs will be lost from view.
poems.n: 759, a time of war: Du Fu spends a night with an old friend, a scholar who never took office. Its power lies in homely detail — the children politely asking where he has come from, spring chives cut in the rain. Shen (Orion) and Shang (Antares) lie on opposite sides of the sky: when one rises, the other has set.

poems.s: day river mountains clouds
z: 王杨卢骆当时体，轻薄为文哂未休。
尔曹身与名俱灭，不废江河万古流。
e: Wang, Yang, Lu, Luo — they wrote in their own day's style;
Glib critics mock their work and never cease to jeer.
But you will perish, body and name, in a little while,
While they, like the great rivers, flow forever here.
poems.n: One of six playful quatrains on literary criticism. The "Four Paragons of the Early Tang" — Wang Bo, Yang Jiong, Lu Zhaolin and Luo Binwang — were sneered at by later critics as old-fashioned. Du Fu's retort is now quoted for any achievement that outlasts its critics.

poems.s: summer river cottage swallows birds two
z: 清江一曲抱村流，长夏江村事事幽。
自去自来梁上燕，相亲相近水中鸥。
老妻画纸为棋局，稚子敲针作钓钩。
但有故人供禄米，微躯此外更何求？
e: A bend of the clear river hugs the village as it flows;
Long summer days in the river village pass in quiet ease.
The swallows on the rafters come and go just as they choose;
The gulls upon the water draw together as they please.
My old wife draws a chessboard on a paper sheet;
My little son is hammering a needle for a hook.
With an old friend to send me rice, my life's complete —
What more could this frail body seek, or where else look?
poems.n: Chengdu, summer 760, at the newly built thatched cottage. After years of war and wandering, Du Fu enjoys a rare peace: swallows and gulls, his wife's homemade chessboard, his son's homemade fish-hook. The rice came from his patron and friend Yan Wu.

poems.te: Song of the Eight Immortals of the Wine Cup
poems.s: day palace cup jar rider
z: 知章骑马似乘船，眼花落井水底眠。
汝阳三斗始朝天，道逢麴车口流涎，恨不移封向酒泉。
左相日兴费万钱，饮如长鲸吸百川，衔杯乐圣称避贤。
宗之潇洒美少年，举觞白眼望青天，皎如玉树临风前。
苏晋长斋绣佛前，醉中往往爱逃禅。
李白一斗诗百篇，长安市上酒家眠。
天子呼来不上船，自称臣是酒中仙。
张旭三杯草圣传，脱帽露顶王公前，挥毫落纸如云烟。
焦遂五斗方卓然，高谈雄辩惊四筵。
e: He Zhizhang sways on horseback as if he's sailing in a boat;
Eyes swimming, he falls down a well, and sleeps on the bottom, content.
The Prince of Ruyang drinks three pecks before he goes to court;
He drools when he meets a brewer's cart along the way he went,
And wishes his fief were moved to the town of Wine Spring.
The Chancellor of the Left spends ten thousand cash a day,
Drinks like a great whale gulping a hundred rivers away;
Cup at his lips, he "loves the sage and shuns the worthy", so they say.
Cui Zongzhi, a handsome youth, so carefree and so free,
Lifts his goblet, rolls his eyes at the blue sky —
Bright as a jade tree standing in the breeze.
Su Jin keeps a long fast before the embroidered Buddha's shrine,
But drunk, he often likes to slip away from Zen to wine.
Li Bai — one peck of wine, a hundred poems!
He sleeps in taverns in Chang'an's market streets.
When the Son of Heaven summons him, he won't board the royal boat:
"Your servant is an immortal of wine," is what he repeats.
Zhang Xu — three cups, and he's the Sage of Cursive Script, it's said;
Before the princes and the lords he takes his cap off, bares his head;
His brush falls on the paper like clouds and mists outspread.
Jiao Sui needs five pecks before he's at his best;
Then his lofty talk and fierce debate astonish every guest.
poems.n: A comic gallery of eight famous drinkers of Chang'an around 740: the poet He Zhizhang, Prince Li Jin of Ruyang, the chancellor Li Shizhi, the dandy Cui Zongzhi, the devout Su Jin, Li Bai, the calligrapher Zhang Xu and the debater Jiao Sui — each sketched in a few lines. The Li Bai lines made his legend. Wine Spring (Jiuquan) is a real town on the Silk Road; "the sage" and "the worthy" were drinkers' slang for clear and cloudy wine; "white eyes" meant looking down on the vulgar.

poems.s: spring river flowers butterfly person
z: 朝回日日典春衣，每日江头尽醉归。
酒债寻常行处有，人生七十古来稀。
穿花蛱蝶深深见，点水蜻蜓款款飞。
传语风光共流转，暂时相赏莫相违。
e: Back from court each day, I pawn my clothes of spring,
And every evening by the river come home drunk as can be.
Wine debts are common — I owe them everywhere I go;
A man who lives to seventy has always been rare to see.
Deep among the flowers the butterflies are glimpsed;
Dipping the water, dragonflies drift slow and free.
I send word to the spring: let us drift on together,
And enjoy each other a while — don't turn away from me.
poems.n: Spring 758, at Qujiang ("Winding River"), the pleasure park of Chang'an. Du Fu, holding a minor post at court, pawns his clothes to drink — less from joy than from disillusion. "Since ancient times, seventy has been rare" gave Chinese the word 古稀 for the age of seventy. (Du Fu himself died at fifty-eight.)

poems.s: autumn cottage two
z: 堂前扑枣任西邻，无食无儿一妇人。
不为困穷宁有此？只缘恐惧转须亲。
即防远客虽多事，便插疏篱却甚真。
已诉征求贫到骨，正思戎马泪盈巾。
e: Let our west neighbour knock the dates down from the tree —
A woman with no food, no children, all alone.
Would she do this if she weren't in poverty?
She's frightened — so be kinder than you've shown.
Her fear of you, a stranger, may be needless, it is true,
But fencing off the tree would make her fears seem right.
She's told me that the levies have bled her to the bone —
I think of war, and tears soak my kerchief through tonight.
poems.n: Du Fu had moved out of his cottage at Kuizhou and lent it to a relative, Mr Wu, who put up a fence to stop a poor widow next door from knocking down dates — as Du Fu had always let her do. This gentle poem-letter asks him to take it down. Few poems anywhere show such quiet, practical compassion.

poems.s: day horse desert wind
z: 胡马大宛名，锋棱瘦骨成。
竹批双耳峻，风入四蹄轻。
所向无空阔，真堪托死生。
骁腾有如此，万里可横行。
e: A western horse, of the famous Ferghana breed,
All sharp edges, built of bone so lean;
Its ears stand pointed like bamboo sliced for speed;
The wind flies in its hooves — so light, so keen.
Wherever it goes, no space is too wide;
You could trust it with your life and with your death.
With such fierce swiftness at your side,
You could ride ten thousand li in a breath.
poems.n: An early poem (c. 740) on a fine horse belonging to an army officer named Fang. Dayuan (Ferghana, in Central Asia) was famous for its "heavenly horses". The horse is also a portrait of the kind of man the young Du Fu hoped to become.

poems.s: night crescent maple river mountains window
z: 死别已吞声，生别常恻恻。
江南瘴疠地，逐客无消息。
故人入我梦，明我长相忆。
恐非平生魂，路远不可测。
魂来枫林青，魂返关塞黑。
君今在罗网，何以有羽翼？
落月满屋梁，犹疑照颜色。
水深波浪阔，无使蛟龙得。
e: A parting by death — one swallows the sobs at last;
A parting in life brings grief that never ends.
South of the River, the fever lands are vast,
And no news comes from the exile, my friend.
Last night you came into my dream,
To show you know I think of you always.
I fear it was no living soul, it would seem —
The road's too long to fathom, all those days.
Your soul came while the maple woods were green;
Your soul went home through mountain passes black.
You're snared in the net — so how, I mean,
Could you have wings to fly here and fly back?
The setting moon floods all the rafters bright;
I half believe it's shining on your face.
The waters are deep, the waves are wide tonight —
Don't let the dragons drag you from your place!
poems.n: 759. Li Bai had been sentenced to exile in Yelang for joining Prince Yong's rebellion, and rumours said he was dead. Du Fu dreams of him and fears the visitor was a ghost. The green maple woods are the south; the black passes, the north where Du Fu lies sleeping. The flood-dragons (蛟龙) are the dangers — and the enemies — on the waters of the south.

poems.te: Song of White Snow: Seeing Judge Wu Off to the Capital
poems.s: winter snow mountains fort flag rider
z: 北风卷地白草折，胡天八月即飞雪。
忽如一夜春风来，千树万树梨花开。
散入珠帘湿罗幕，狐裘不暖锦衾薄。
将军角弓不得控，都护铁衣冷难着。
瀚海阑干百丈冰，愁云惨淡万里凝。
中军置酒饮归客，胡琴琵琶与羌笛。
纷纷暮雪下辕门，风掣红旗冻不翻。
轮台东门送君去，去时雪满天山路。
山回路转不见君，雪上空留马行处。
e: The north wind rolls the land and snaps the white grass low;
In the eighth month, the northern sky is flying thick with snow.
As if, in a single night, the breeze of spring had come,
A thousand trees, ten thousand trees, burst into pear-blossom.
It drifts through pearl curtains, soaks the silken tent within;
Fox furs give no warmth, and brocade quilts seem thin.
The general cannot draw his horn-bow, stiff with cold;
The Protector's iron armour is too chill to hold.
The desert sea is cracked with ice a hundred fathoms high;
Gloomy clouds, ten thousand li, are frozen as they lie.
In the central tent we set out wine to toast the parting guest,
With Hu fiddles, pipas and Qiang flutes playing their best.
At dusk the snow falls thick and fast upon the camp's front gate;
The red flag, frozen stiff, won't flutter in the wind's weight.
By Luntai's eastern gate I see you on your way;
Snow fills the road across the Tianshan as you leave today.
The mountain bends, the road turns, and you're lost from view;
Only hoofprints in the snow remain, where your horse went through.
poems.n: Luntai, in today's Xinjiang, 754: Cen Shen sees off a colleague returning to Chang'an. Snow arriving overnight like pear blossom on a spring wind is the most famous snow image in Chinese poetry. The ending — the friend gone, only hoofprints left in the snow — is pure longing.

poems.te: Meeting an Envoy Bound for the Capital
poems.s: day desert rider horse two
z: 故园东望路漫漫，双袖龙钟泪不干。
马上相逢无纸笔，凭君传语报平安。
e: I gaze east toward my home — the road goes on and on;
Both my sleeves are soaked with tears that never dry.
We meet on horseback — no brush, no paper, none;
Please tell my family I'm safe and well, as you pass by.
poems.n: On his way to the Central Asian frontier in 749, Cen Shen meets an envoy heading back to Chang'an. No time to write — only a spoken message: "I'm safe." The simplest words carry the deepest feeling.

poems.s: dusk desert moon rider horse
z: 走马西来欲到天，辞家见月两回圆。
今夜不知何处宿，平沙万里绝人烟。
e: I ride west till it seems I'll reach the edge of the sky;
Twice since I left my home I've seen the moon grow round.
Tonight I do not know where I shall lie —
Ten thousand li of sand, and not a hearth-smoke to be found.
poems.n: Crossing the Gobi (碛) in 749. Two full moons measure two months away from home; the endless sand without "the smoke of human fires" measures the loneliness.

poems.te: On the March at the Double Ninth, Thinking of My Garden in Chang'an
poems.s: autumn chrysanthemum fort flag hills
z: 强欲登高去，无人送酒来。
遥怜故园菊，应傍战场开。
e: I force myself to climb the heights today,
But no one's here to bring me any wine.
I think with pity of my garden's flowers far away —
They must be blooming by the battle line.
poems.n: The Double Ninth festival of 757, with the army in the field; Chang'an, Cen Shen's home, was in rebel hands. Instead of drinking chrysanthemum wine with friends, he imagines the chrysanthemums of his abandoned garden flowering beside the fighting. Tao Yuanming once sat out this festival with no wine until a friend sent some; here, no one does.

poems.s: night spring window river crescent
z: 洞房昨夜春风起，遥忆美人湘江水。
枕上片时春梦中，行尽江南数千里。
e: Last night the spring wind stirred inside my chamber's door;
I thought of my love, far off by the Xiang River's shore.
Upon my pillow, in a moment's dream of spring,
I travelled thousands of li south of the Yangtze, and more.
poems.n: A lovely paradox of time and distance: a dream lasting a moment covers thousands of li to reach a loved one. "Spring dream" (春梦) is also an image of fleeting happiness.

poems.s: night crescent pine grass wind rider
z: 林暗草惊风，将军夜引弓。
平明寻白羽，没在石棱中。
e: Dark woods; the grass starts up as wind sweeps by;
The general draws his bow at dead of night.
At dawn they seek his white-fletched arrow — why,
It's buried in a rock, sunk out of sight!
poems.n: Based on a story of the Han general Li Guang, who shot at what he took for a tiger in the dark grass — and in the morning found his arrow buried in a rock. The "grass startled by wind" hints at the tiger without naming it.

poems.s: night winter snow geese rider horse
z: 月黑雁飞高，单于夜遁逃。
欲将轻骑逐，大雪满弓刀。
e: No moon; the wild geese fly up high and far;
The khan has fled, escaping in the night.
We'd chase him down with our light horse —
Heavy snow covers bows and blades in white.
poems.n: The night is so dark that the khan's escape is known only from the startled geese. The last line — the cavalry poised, snow piling on their weapons — freezes the moment before the chase.

poems.te: Hearing a Flute at Night on the Wall of Shouxiang
poems.s: night moon desert fort frost
z: 回乐烽前沙似雪，受降城外月如霜。
不知何处吹芦管，一夜征人尽望乡。
e: Before Huile's beacon tower, the sand lies white as snow;
Outside the Surrender City walls, the moon is like the frost.
From somewhere — who knows where? — a reed pipe's playing low;
All night the soldiers gaze toward home, and feel what they have lost.
poems.n: Shouxiang ("Accepting Surrender") was a fortress on the Yellow River in the far north. Sand and moonlight turn the world white; an unseen reed pipe plays; every soldier turns toward home. Set to music, the poem was sung all over the empire.

poems.s: day river boat person
z: 嫁得瞿塘贾，朝朝误妾期。
早知潮有信，嫁与弄潮儿。
e: I married a merchant of Qutang Gorge;
Every day he breaks his word to me.
Had I known the tide keeps faith so true,
I'd have wed a boy who rides the tides at sea.
poems.n: A merchant's wife, in the voice of a southern folk song. The tide comes back on time, every time; her husband never does — so she'd rather have married one of the young men who play in the great tidal bore of the Qiantang River. Funny and sad at once.

poems.te: Grass on the Ancient Plain: A Farewell
poems.s: spring grass hills wall two rider
z: 离离原上草，一岁一枯荣。
野火烧不尽，春风吹又生。
远芳侵古道，晴翠接荒城。
又送王孙去，萋萋满别情。
e: How lush the grass upon the plain!
Each year it withers, then grows green again.
The wildfires cannot burn it all away;
The spring wind blows, and it springs back to stay.
Its distant fragrance creeps across the ancient road;
Its sunlit green runs to the ruined town's abode.
Once more I see a friend go on his way —
The grass grows thick with all I cannot say.
poems.n: Written at sixteen as an exercise on a set theme ("Composed on the Theme…", 赋得). When the young Bai Juyi brought his poems to the capital, the writer Gu Kuang joked about his name — "Juyi" means "living easily", and "rice is dear in Chang'an; living here is not easy" — until he read the second couplet and exclaimed, "With lines like these, living here will be easy!" "Wildfire cannot burn it out; the spring wind blows and it grows again" became a proverb for indomitable life.

poems.s: dawn spring sun river flowers willow boat
z: 江南好，风景旧曾谙。
日出江花红胜火，春来江水绿如蓝。
能不忆江南？
e: The South is fair —
Its scenery I knew so well:
At sunrise, riverside flowers redder than fire;
In spring, the river's water green as indigo's spell.
How could I not remember the South?
poems.n: Written in old age in Luoyang, remembering his years as governor of Hangzhou and Suzhou. One of the earliest *ci* lyrics by a major poet, set to the tune "Remembering the South". The colours — fire-red and indigo-green — are pure and intense, like memory itself.

poems.te: A Spring Walk by Qiantang Lake
poems.s: spring lake willow swallows oriole flowers horse temple
z: 孤山寺北贾亭西，水面初平云脚低。
几处早莺争暖树，谁家新燕啄春泥。
乱花渐欲迷人眼，浅草才能没马蹄。
最爱湖东行不足，绿杨阴里白沙堤。
e: North of Gushan Temple, west of Lord Jia's pavilion,
The lake has just come level; the clouds hang low and near.
Here and there, early orioles vie for sunny trees;
Whose new swallows peck the spring mud here?
A riot of flowers begins to dazzle the eye;
The tender grass just covers the horses' hooves.
Best I love the lake's east side — I can't walk it enough:
The white-sand causeway in the green willows' shade it moves.
poems.n: Hangzhou's West Lake (then called Qiantang Lake) in early spring, when Bai Juyi was its governor (822–824). Every detail is "just beginning" — early orioles, new swallows, grass just tall enough to hide a hoof. The Bai Causeway, the white-sand dyke he loved, still carries his name.

poems.te: Song of the River at Dusk
poems.s: dusk autumn sun river crescent
z: 一道残阳铺水中，半江瑟瑟半江红。
可怜九月初三夜，露似真珠月似弓。
e: A ray of the setting sun lies spread across the stream:
Half the river emerald-cold, and half aglow with red.
How lovely is this night, the third of the ninth moon:
Dew like real pearls; the moon a bow overhead.
poems.n: Two pictures in one quatrain: sunset with the river half in shadow (瑟瑟, the blue-green of a precious stone) and half aflame; then night, with dewdrops like pearls and a slender crescent moon like a drawn bow.

poems.s: spring peach temple mountains clouds
z: 人间四月芳菲尽，山寺桃花始盛开。
长恨春归无觅处，不知转入此中来。
e: In the world below, the April flowers are gone;
At this mountain temple, peach blossoms just begin.
I always grieved that spring went off and left no trace —
Not knowing it had come up here, and settled in.
poems.n: Mount Lu, 817. High on the mountain the season lags behind the plain, so the poet finds spring still in full bloom. The small scientific observation becomes a happy surprise: spring has not vanished — it simply climbed the mountain.

poems.te: A Question for Liu the Nineteenth
poems.s: dusk winter snow cottage jar cup window
z: 绿蚁新醅酒，红泥小火炉。
晚来天欲雪，能饮一杯无？
e: New-brewed wine with green froth like ants;
A little stove of red clay, burning low.
Evening falls, and the sky threatens snow —
Will you come and drink a cup or no?
poems.n: A tiny invitation that every Chinese reader treasures: the "green ants" are the bubbles floating on fresh unfiltered rice wine; the red stove glows; snow is coming. Who could refuse?

poems.s: winter snow mountains wall rider smoke
z: 卖炭翁，伐薪烧炭南山中。
满面尘灰烟火色，两鬓苍苍十指黑。
卖炭得钱何所营？身上衣裳口中食。
可怜身上衣正单，心忧炭贱愿天寒。
夜来城外一尺雪，晓驾炭车辗冰辙。
牛困人饥日已高，市南门外泥中歇。
翩翩两骑来是谁？黄衣使者白衫儿。
手把文书口称敕，回车叱牛牵向北。
一车炭，千余斤，宫使驱将惜不得。
半匹红绡一丈绫，系向牛头充炭直。
e: The old charcoal seller
Cuts wood and burns charcoal in the Southern Hills.
His face is grimed with dust and ash, the colour of smoke and fire;
His temples are grey, his ten fingers black as the coal he fills.
What does he want with the money he gets for his charcoal?
Clothes on his back and food in his mouth — no more.
Pitiful — his clothes are thin, and yet
He hopes for cold, afraid the price will be poor.
Last night a foot of snow fell outside the town;
At dawn he drives his cart through ruts of ice.
The ox is weary, he is hungry, the sun is high;
He rests in the mud outside the south market gate, to wait a price.
Who are those two riders, prancing on their way?
A eunuch in yellow, and his boy in white.
Document in hand, they shout, "Imperial decree!"
And turn the cart, and drive the ox north, out of sight.
A cartload of charcoal — over a thousand pounds —
The palace envoys drive it off; he can't hold on.
Half a bolt of red gauze and ten feet of silk
They tie to the ox's head as payment — and are gone.
poems.n: One of Bai Juyi's *New Yuefu*, written to expose abuses. Palace eunuchs would "buy" goods in the markets of Chang'an at whatever price they liked. The old man's wish — cold weather, though he is freezing — is one of the most poignant lines in Chinese. A worthless scrap of silk pays for his whole winter's labour.

poems.s: summer lotus lake boat person
z: 小娃撑小艇，偷采白莲回。
不解藏踪迹，浮萍一道开。
e: A little child poles a little boat,
Sneaking home with white lotus she has picked.
She hasn't learned to hide her tracks —
Through the duckweed, a clear path has been flicked.
poems.n: A comic snapshot: the child thinks the theft is secret, but the open lane through the floating duckweed gives her away.

poems.s: night winter snow bamboo window cottage
z: 已讶衾枕冷，复见窗户明。
夜深知雪重，时闻折竹声。
e: I'm surprised my quilt and pillow are so cold,
Then see the window has grown bright.
Deep in the night, I know the snow is heavy:
Now and then, I hear bamboo snap in the night.
poems.n: Snow is never seen directly: it is felt as cold, seen as a glow on the window-paper, and heard as bamboo stems cracking under its weight.

poems.s: night autumn moon fields frost cottage
z: 霜草苍苍虫切切，村南村北行人绝。
独出前门望野田，月明荞麦花如雪。
e: Frosted grass is grey; the insects chirr and chirr;
South of the village, north of it, no traveller can be seen.
Alone I step out of my gate to gaze at the fields:
In the moonlight, buckwheat flowers are white as snow, serene.
poems.n: 811, when Bai Juyi was at his family home in mourning for his mother. Grey, silent, lonely — and then a sudden whiteness of moonlit buckwheat blossoms brightens the whole poem.

poems.te: A Flower That Is Not a Flower
poems.s: night mist clouds flowers moon
z: 花非花，雾非雾。
夜半来，天明去。
来如春梦几多时？去似朝云无觅处。
e: A flower, yet not a flower;
A mist, yet not a mist.
She comes at midnight,
She leaves at dawn's first tryst.
She comes like a spring dream — how long can it last?
She goes like morning cloud, gone without trace, gone past.
poems.n: A riddling love song with no subject named — a lover's secret visits, perhaps, or a dream, or life itself. The "morning cloud" recalls the goddess of Mount Wu, who visited a king in his dream and was "morning cloud and evening rain".

poems.s: night moon river tower hills person
z: 汴水流，泗水流，流到瓜州古渡头。
吴山点点愁。
思悠悠，恨悠悠，恨到归时方始休。
月明人倚楼。
e: The Bian flows on, the Si flows on,
Flowing to Guazhou's ancient ferry stair;
The hills of Wu, dot after dot, are sorrow there.
Longing, so long — regret, so long —
Regret that ends only when he comes home again.
In the bright moon, she leans on the tower stair.
poems.n: An early *ci* lyric with a folk-song lilt. A woman follows in her mind the rivers her man travelled down, all the way to the ferry at Guazhou on the Yangtze; even the distant hills of Wu look like spots of grief. The repetitions (流…流, 悠悠…悠悠) imitate both the rivers and the endlessness of longing.

poems.s: night autumn moon temple pavilion river
z: 江南忆，最忆是杭州。
山寺月中寻桂子，郡亭枕上看潮头。
何日更重游？
e: Of the South, what I remember best
Is Hangzhou, above all the rest:
At the hill temple, seeking cassia seeds beneath the moon;
At the prefect's pavilion, on my pillow, watching the tide's crest.
When shall I go back on that quest?
poems.n: Legend said that cassia seeds fell from the moon (where a cassia tree grows) around Hangzhou's Lingyin Temple each autumn. The tidal bore of the Qiantang River, which could be watched from the governor's pavilion, is one of the great sights of China.

poems.s: night palace candle window
z: 泪湿罗巾梦不成，夜深前殿按歌声。
红颜未老恩先断，斜倚熏笼坐到明。
e: Tears soak her silk handkerchief; she cannot sleep or dream;
Deep in the night, from the front hall, comes music and song.
Her rosy face not yet old, the emperor's favour's gone;
She leans on the incense cage, and sits there all night long.
poems.n: One of three thousand palace women, forgotten while the emperor feasts in the front hall with another. The incense cage (熏笼) was a basket over a brazier used to warm and perfume clothes — the only warmth she has left.

poems.te: Thinking of Home on the Winter Solstice at Handan
poems.s: night winter candle cottage person
z: 邯郸驿里逢冬至，抱膝灯前影伴身。
想得家中夜深坐，还应说着远行人。
e: At the Handan post-station, the Winter Solstice comes;
Hugging my knees by the lamp, my shadow keeps me company.
I picture my family at home, sitting up late tonight —
They must be talking of the one who's far away: of me.
poems.n: The Winter Solstice was one of the great family festivals of the Tang. Like Wang Wei's Double Ninth poem, the homesickness is turned around: he imagines them missing him.

poems.s: summer sun fields person two
z: 田家少闲月，五月人倍忙。
夜来南风起，小麦覆陇黄。
妇姑荷箪食，童稚携壶浆，
相随饷田去，丁壮在南冈。
足蒸暑土气，背灼炎天光，
力尽不知热，但惜夏日长。
复有贫妇人，抱子在其旁，
右手秉遗穗，左臂悬敝筐。
听其相顾言，闻者为悲伤。
家田输税尽，拾此充饥肠。
今我何功德？曾不事农桑。
吏禄三百石，岁晏有余粮。
念此私自愧，尽日不能忘。
e: Farm families have few idle months;
In the fifth month they're twice as busy as before.
Last night the south wind rose, and now
The ripe wheat covers the ridges, yellow to the core.
Wives and mothers carry baskets of food;
The children bring jugs of gruel along;
Together they take the meal to the fields,
Where the men toil on the southern ridge, strong.
Their feet are steamed by the hot earth;
Their backs are scorched by the blazing sun;
Worn out, they don't even feel the heat,
And only wish the long summer day weren't done.
And there's a poor woman, too,
With a baby in her arms, beside the rest;
In her right hand, the ears of grain she's gleaned;
On her left arm, a broken basket pressed.
I hear her talking with the others —
Whoever hears her grieves:
"Our own fields all went to pay the tax;
I glean these to fill our stomachs with the sheaves."
And what merit have I, I ask myself?
I've never farmed or tended silk.
My salary is three hundred bushels;
At year's end, I've grain to spare, and milk.
Thinking of this, I'm secretly ashamed,
And all day long I can't forget the shame I bear.
poems.n: 806, when Bai Juyi was a county magistrate near Chang'an. The farmers want the day to be longer so they can harvest more, though it is killing them; the gleaning widow has lost her land to taxes. The poem's last lines — an official confessing he has done nothing to deserve his salary — are rare and remarkable in any literature.

poems.s: day mountains pine person
z: 赠君一法决狐疑，不用钻龟与祝蓍。
试玉要烧三日满，辨材须待七年期。
周公恐惧流言日，王莽谦恭未篡时。
向使当初身便死，一生真伪复谁知？
e: I'll give you a way to settle every doubt
Without cracking tortoise shells or casting yarrow stalks:
To test true jade, you burn it three whole days;
To judge good timber, wait seven years — then talk.
The Duke of Zhou lived in fear when rumours spread;
Wang Mang seemed humble — till he seized the throne.
Had either died before the truth came out,
Who would have known what each one was? Who'd have known?
poems.n: Written in exile in 815. True jade survives three days in fire; the camphor tree is only distinguishable from a lesser tree after seven years of growth. The Duke of Zhou, the most loyal of regents, was rumoured to be plotting usurpation; Wang Mang, who did usurp the Han throne, was famous for his humility beforehand. Only time reveals the truth of a person.

poems.s: summer lotus lake boat person
z: 菱叶萦波荷飐风，荷花深处小船通。
逢郎欲语低头笑，碧玉搔头落水中。
e: Water-chestnut leaves twine on the waves; lotus sways in the wind;
Deep among the lotus blooms, a little boat glides through.
She meets her young man, wants to speak — lowers her head and smiles,
And her green jade hairpin slips into the water, too.
poems.n: A lotus-gathering girl meets her sweetheart; too shy to speak, she bows her head — and loses her hairpin in the lake. The tiny accident says everything about her flustered heart.

poems.s: autumn river boat willow two wind
z: 南浦凄凄别，西风袅袅秋。
一看肠一断，好去莫回头。
e: At South Shore, a sad farewell;
The west wind sighs — it's autumn now.
Each look back breaks my heart once more —
Go well, and don't look back somehow.
poems.n: South Shore (南浦) was a stock name for a place of parting, from the *Songs of Chu*: "I see you off at the southern shore." The simple, broken plea — "go well, don't turn your head" — is because every glance back is another heartbreak.

poems.te: Reading Yuan the Ninth's Poems in My Boat
poems.s: night river boat candle wind
z: 把君诗卷灯前读，诗尽灯残天未明。
眼痛灭灯犹暗坐，逆风吹浪打船声。
e: I read your book of poems by the lamp;
The poems end, the lamp burns low — still not yet dawn.
My eyes ache; I put the lamp out, sit on in the dark;
Against the wind, the waves strike the boat on and on.
poems.n: 815: Bai Juyi, on his way into exile at Jiangzhou, reads the poems of his dearest friend Yuan Zhen, himself in exile. The wind and waves battering the boat in the dark stand for the storms that have scattered them both.

poems.s: night moon palace clouds mist pavilion
z: 汉皇重色思倾国，御宇多年求不得。
杨家有女初长成，养在深闺人未识。
天生丽质难自弃，一朝选在君王侧。
回眸一笑百媚生，六宫粉黛无颜色。
春寒赐浴华清池，温泉水滑洗凝脂。
侍儿扶起娇无力，始是新承恩泽时。
云鬓花颜金步摇，芙蓉帐暖度春宵。
春宵苦短日高起，从此君王不早朝。
承欢侍宴无闲暇，春从春游夜专夜。
后宫佳丽三千人，三千宠爱在一身。
金屋妆成娇侍夜，玉楼宴罢醉和春。
姊妹弟兄皆列土，可怜光彩生门户。
遂令天下父母心，不重生男重生女。
骊宫高处入青云，仙乐风飘处处闻。
缓歌慢舞凝丝竹，尽日君王看不足。
渔阳鼙鼓动地来，惊破霓裳羽衣曲。
九重城阙烟尘生，千乘万骑西南行。
翠华摇摇行复止，西出都门百余里。
六军不发无奈何，宛转蛾眉马前死。
花钿委地无人收，翠翘金雀玉搔头。
君王掩面救不得，回看血泪相和流。
黄埃散漫风萧索，云栈萦纡登剑阁。
峨嵋山下少人行，旌旗无光日色薄。
蜀江水碧蜀山青，圣主朝朝暮暮情。
行宫见月伤心色，夜雨闻铃肠断声。
天旋地转回龙驭，到此踌躇不能去。
马嵬坡下泥土中，不见玉颜空死处。
君臣相顾尽沾衣，东望都门信马归。
归来池苑皆依旧，太液芙蓉未央柳。
芙蓉如面柳如眉，对此如何不泪垂。
春风桃李花开日，秋雨梧桐叶落时。
西宫南内多秋草，落叶满阶红不扫。
梨园弟子白发新，椒房阿监青娥老。
夕殿萤飞思悄然，孤灯挑尽未成眠。
迟迟钟鼓初长夜，耿耿星河欲曙天。
鸳鸯瓦冷霜华重，翡翠衾寒谁与共。
悠悠生死别经年，魂魄不曾来入梦。
临邛道士鸿都客，能以精诚致魂魄。
为感君王辗转思，遂教方士殷勤觅。
排空驭气奔如电，升天入地求之遍。
上穷碧落下黄泉，两处茫茫皆不见。
忽闻海上有仙山，山在虚无缥渺间。
楼阁玲珑五云起，其中绰约多仙子。
中有一人字太真，雪肤花貌参差是。
金阙西厢叩玉扃，转教小玉报双成。
闻道汉家天子使，九华帐里梦魂惊。
揽衣推枕起徘徊，珠箔银屏迤逦开。
云鬓半偏新睡觉，花冠不整下堂来。
风吹仙袂飘飘举，犹似霓裳羽衣舞。
玉容寂寞泪阑干，梨花一枝春带雨。
含情凝睇谢君王，一别音容两渺茫。
昭阳殿里恩爱绝，蓬莱宫中日月长。
回头下望人寰处，不见长安见尘雾。
惟将旧物表深情，钿合金钗寄将去。
钗留一股合一扇，钗擘黄金合分钿。
但教心似金钿坚，天上人间会相见。
临别殷勤重寄词，词中有誓两心知。
七月七日长生殿，夜半无人私语时。
在天愿作比翼鸟，在地愿为连理枝。
天长地久有时尽，此恨绵绵无绝期。
e: The Han emperor prized beauty, longed for one to topple states;
Through all his years upon the throne, he sought and found no mate.
The Yang clan had a daughter who was just in her first bloom,
Raised deep within the women's rooms, unknown beyond her room.
But beauty given by heaven is hard to hide away:
She was chosen for the sovereign's side one day.
She turned her head and smiled — a hundred charms were born;
The painted ladies of the Six Palaces looked colourless and worn.
In the chill of spring he let her bathe in Huaqing's waters fine;
The silken springs washed over skin like cream, divine.
Her maids helped her up, so delicate, so weak —
That was when the emperor's favour first touched her cheek.
Cloud-like hair, a flowered face, a golden hairpin's swing;
Behind warm lotus curtains they spent the nights of spring.
Spring nights were all too short; he rose when the sun was high;
From then on he held no morning court — he let the dawns go by.
She shared his feasts and pleasures, never with an hour to rest;
In spring she joined his spring rides; night after night she was his guest.
Three thousand beauties filled the inner palace halls;
The love meant for three thousand on one woman falls.
In her Golden House, made up, she charmed him through the night;
At the Jade Tower, the feasting done, she was drunk with spring's delight.
Her sisters and her brothers all were granted lands and fame —
How dazzling was the glory shining on her family's name!
So parents everywhere beneath the sky now changed their mind:
Not sons, but daughters, were the children they most hoped to find.
High on Mount Li, the palace rose into the blue clouds' height;
Immortal music on the wind was heard there, day and night.
Slow songs, unhurried dances held the strings and flutes in thrall;
All day the sovereign watched, and never had enough at all.
Then the war-drums of Yuyang came, shaking the ground,
And shattered "Rainbow Skirt and Feathered Coat" with their sound.
Smoke and dust rose from the nine-walled city's towers;
A thousand chariots, ten thousand riders fled southwest in those hours.
The kingfisher banners swayed; they marched and stopped once more,
A hundred li out west, beyond the capital's door.
The Six Armies would not march — what could be done?
Before the horses, the moth-browed beauty died, her struggle done.
Her flowered ornaments lay where they fell, and no one gathered them:
Kingfisher plumes, gold sparrows, and a jade pin's broken stem.
The sovereign hid his face — he could not save her, try as he might;
Looking back, his tears and blood flowed mingled at the sight.
Yellow dust blew all around; the wind was bleak and sere;
By cloud-high plank roads winding, they climbed to Sword Pavilion here.
Below Mount Emei, few travellers came by;
The banners lost their lustre, and the sun grew pale in the sky.
The rivers of Shu are green, the mountains of Shu are blue;
Morning and evening, the sovereign's longing grew.
In his travelling palace, the moon was heartbreak to see;
In night rain, the harness bells rang out in agony.
The world turned round; the dragon carriage was coming home at last;
Reaching here, he hesitated, and could not go past.
Beneath the slope of Mawei, in the mud and clay,
No jade face could be seen — just the empty place she lay.
Lord and ministers looked at each other, tears soaking every gown;
Eastward, they let the horses find their own way back to town.
Returning, the pools and gardens were all as they had been —
The lotus of Taiye Lake, the willows of Weiyang green.
The lotus was like her face, the willow like her brow —
Facing them, how could his tears not fall now?
In spring winds, when the peach and plum trees bloom;
In autumn rains, when wutong leaves fall through the gloom;
The Western Palace and the Southern Court were deep in autumn grass;
Red leaves lay thick upon the steps, unswept, as seasons pass.
The players of the Pear Garden had hair turned newly white;
The maids of the Pepper Chamber had lost their youthful light.
In the evening hall fireflies flitted; he sat in silent thought;
He trimmed his lonely lamp till it burned out — but sleep came not.
Slow, slow the bells and drums began the long night's span;
Bright, bright the Milky Way, before the dawn began.
The mandarin-duck roof tiles were cold, the frost lay thick and fair;
The kingfisher quilt was chill — and who was there to share?
Distant, distant, life and death apart through all the years —
Her soul had never come into his dreams to dry his tears.
A Daoist priest from Linqiong, a guest at the capital gate,
Could summon spirits of the dead by his devotion's weight.
Moved by the sovereign's tossing, turning longing and his pain,
They sent this master out to search with all his might and main.
He split the sky and rode the wind, as swift as lightning flies;
He searched the depths beneath the earth, and searched the highest skies —
Up to the blue void, down to the Yellow Springs below:
Both were vast and empty; she was nowhere, high or low.
Then he heard of an immortal mountain in the sea,
A mountain set amid the void, in misty mystery.
Its exquisite towers rose where five-coloured clouds unfurled;
Within lived many graceful fairies, far beyond the world.
And one among them bore the name of Taizhen, so they said,
With snowy skin and flower face — much like the one now dead.
At the golden palace's west wing, he knocked on the door of jade,
And asked Little Jade to tell Shuangcheng, who would tell the lady's maid.
Hearing that an envoy of the Han emperor had come,
Within her nine-flowered curtains, her dreaming soul was struck dumb.
She pushed her pillow, caught her robe, rose up and paced the floor;
The pearl blinds and the silver screens unfolded, door by door.
Her cloud of hair hung half aside — she had only just awoken;
Her flower crown askew, she came down the hall, her calm all broken.
The wind blew her immortal sleeves; they fluttered as she swayed,
As though "Rainbow Skirt and Feathered Coat" were being played.
Her jade-white face was lonely, tears streaming without end —
A spray of pear blossom in spring rain, beneath the drops to bend.
Gazing with deep feeling, she thanked her sovereign lord:
"Since we parted, voice and face are lost — no word, no sight restored.
In Zhaoyang Hall, our love and favour have been cut;
In Penglai Palace, days and months are long, the door is shut.
I turn my head and look down toward the world of men —
I cannot see Chang'an, only dust and mist again.
Let these old keepsakes show you that my love is true:
This inlaid box and golden hairpin — take them back with you.
One prong of the hairpin I keep, one half of the box I hold:
I break the hairpin's gold in two, and split the inlaid gold.
If only our hearts stay as firm as gold and inlay are,
In heaven or on earth we'll meet again, however far."
At parting she sent words again, with care, for him to bear;
In them was a vow known only to the two who'd shared it there:
"On the seventh of the seventh month, in the Hall of Long Life,
At midnight, when no one was near, we whispered, man and wife:
'In heaven, may we be two birds that fly wing to wing;
On earth, two trees whose branches intertwine and cling.'"
Heaven is long and earth endures, yet both will one day end —
But this sorrow will go on forever, and never mend.
poems.n: Written in 806, when Bai Juyi was thirty-four: the love of Emperor Xuanzong (thinly disguised as "the Han emperor") and Consort Yang Guifei — her rise, the An Lushan rebellion (the "war-drums of Yuyang"), the flight to Sichuan, the mutinous troops at Mawei who demanded her death, the emperor's endless grief, and a Daoist magician who finds her soul on an island of immortals. Her vow — to be "birds flying wing to wing, branches intertwined" (比翼鸟, 连理枝) — is the most famous pledge of love in Chinese, and the closing couplet gave the poem its title.

poems.s: night autumn moon river boat maple reeds two
z: 浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁？
琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为《霓裳》后《六幺》。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？
杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？
呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作《琵琶行》。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？
江州司马青衫湿。
e: By the Xunyang River, at night, I saw a guest away;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn grey.
I, the host, dismounted; my guest was in his boat;
We raised our cups to drink — but there was no music, not one note.
Drunk, yet joyless, sadly we were about to part;
At parting, the moon lay steeped in the boundless river's heart.
Then suddenly, across the water, came a pipa's sound;
The host forgot to leave; the guest stayed, outward-bound.
We followed the sound and softly asked who it was that played;
The pipa stopped; she was slow to answer, and delayed.
We moved our boat beside hers and asked her to appear;
We poured more wine, relit the lamps, and spread the feast with cheer.
At last, after a thousand pleas, she came out with slow grace,
Still holding up her pipa so it half-concealed her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings — a note or two, or three;
Before a tune had even formed, there was feeling, plain to see.
Each string was muffled, every note was heavy with thought,
As if she told a lifetime's grief, of hopes that came to naught.
Head bowed, she let her hand play on, continuing on and on,
And told the countless sorrows of her heart, one by one.
Lightly she pressed and slowly twisted, swept, and plucked the strings:
First "Rainbow Skirt", then "Green Waist" — the tunes of courts and kings.
The heavy strings roared like a sudden squall of rain;
The fine strings murmured like lovers' whispers, low and plain.
Roaring and murmuring, interwoven as she played —
Like pearls, both large and small, that fall upon a plate of jade.
Now orioles chattered, liquid, gliding under flowers;
Now a choked spring sobbed, struggling under ice for hours.
The icy spring grew cold and halting; the strings congealed and died;
Congealed, cut off, the sound fell still — the music paused, held still inside.
A different, deeper sorrow, a hidden grief, was born:
Now silence spoke more eloquently than sound — and more forlorn.
Then suddenly a silver vase burst, and water splashed about;
Armoured horsemen charged, and swords and spears rang out.
The tune ended: she swept her plectrum across the strings' heart;
The four strings cried as one, like silk being torn apart.
On boats to east and west, a hush; no one spoke at all —
Only the autumn moon, white in mid-river, over all.
Thoughtfully she laid the plectrum down between the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, composed her face, and spoke of things:
"I was a girl of the capital once," she said. "My home
Was down by Toad Mound — that's where I used to roam.
At thirteen I had learned to play the pipa with full skill;
My name stood in the first rank of the Music Academy's bill.
My playing made the master musicians bow in admiration;
My beauty, when made up, roused even Qiuniang's indignation.
The young lords of the Five Tombs vied to shower me with gifts;
For one song, rolls of red silk past counting, piled in drifts.
Silver combs with jewelled heads broke as they beat the time;
Blood-red silk skirts were stained with spilt wine — I was in my prime.
This year was laughter, and the next year laughter too;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed, and idly through.
My brother joined the army, and the madam passed away;
Evenings went and mornings came; my looks faded day by day.
Before my door it grew deserted; fewer horses came;
Grown old, I married a merchant, and took a merchant's name.
A merchant cares for profit, and thinks little of goodbye;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea, and left me by.
Since then, at the river's mouth, I guard the empty boat;
Around it, bright moonlight; the river cold, remote.
Late at night I suddenly dreamed of my young days;
I wept in my dream, and red tears through my rouge ran in a glaze."
Hearing the pipa, I had sighed already, deep;
Hearing her story, I sighed again, and began to weep.
We both are outcasts, drifting at the far ends of the earth;
Meeting like this, what need to have known each other since our birth?
"Since last year I left the capital, I've lived in banishment;
I lie here sick in Xunyang town, where I was demoted and sent.
Xunyang is remote, and there's no music to be found;
All year I've never heard the strings or flutes resound.
I live beside the Pen, where the ground is low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my house like a camp.
What do I hear here, morning and evening long?
The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbons' mournful song.
On spring river mornings full of flowers, on autumn nights of moon,
I often take my wine and drink alone, and end too soon.
Of course there are hill songs and village flutes — but they
Are shrill and harsh and croaking, painful when they play.
Tonight I heard your pipa speak, and it seemed
Like heavenly music — my ears for a while were redeemed.
Don't refuse; sit down again and play us one more song,
And I will write for you 'The Ballad of the Pipa' before long."
Moved by what I said, she stood a long while there,
Then sat, and tightened the strings; the notes grew quick and spare.
So mournful, so unlike the music played before,
That all who heard it hid their faces, weeping once more.
And of them all, whose tears were falling most? I'd say
The Marshal of Jiangzhou's — his blue robe soaked that day.
poems.n: Written in 816 at Jiangzhou (Jiujiang), where Bai Juyi had been demoted to the empty post of marshal (司马). Seeing a friend off on the river at night, he hears a former star musician of the capital, now a merchant's neglected wife. The description of her playing — "large pearls and small pearls falling on a plate of jade", "now silence was more eloquent than sound", "a silver vase bursting" — is the most famous evocation of music in Chinese. "We are both outcasts at the ends of the earth; why must we have known each other before?" became the motto of every exile. Blue-green robes were worn by the lowest-ranking officials.

poems.s: spring rain peach cottage person
z: 清明时节雨纷纷，路上行人欲断魂。
借问酒家何处有？牧童遥指杏花村。
e: The Qingming rain comes drizzling down without an end;
The travellers on the road are lost in grief, heart-sore.
"Where can I find a tavern?" I ask — and round the bend,
A herd-boy points far off to Apricot Village's door.
