poems.n: Qingming ("Clear and Bright", early April) is the festival for sweeping ancestors' graves — a day of mourning, traditionally wet. The tavern and the apricot blossoms promise a little warmth. "Apricot Blossom Village" (杏花村) became the name of a famous liquor, and several towns still claim to be the place.

poems.s: dusk autumn mountains maple clouds cottage rider
z: 远上寒山石径斜，白云生处有人家。
停车坐爱枫林晚，霜叶红于二月花。
e: Far up the cold mountain, a stone path slants and climbs;
Where the white clouds rise, there are homes of people too.
I stop my carriage: I love the maple woods at evening time —
The frosted leaves are redder than spring flowers ever grew.
poems.n: The great autumn poem: Du Mu stops simply to look. The last line overturns the usual melancholy of autumn — frost-touched maples outshine even the flowers of the second month of spring. (坐 here means "because".)

poems.s: spring rain temple flag oriole river mist
z: 千里莺啼绿映红，水村山郭酒旗风。
南朝四百八十寺，多少楼台烟雨中。
e: A thousand li of orioles; the green sets off the red;
Wine pennants flutter in the wind by river towns and hills.
Four hundred eighty temples the Southern Dynasties spread —
How many towers stand in the misty rain there still?
poems.n: The whole of the south in spring, in fourteen characters — then history. The Southern Dynasties (420–589) built hundreds of temples around Nanjing; their emperors' piety did not save them. The temples stand silent in the rain, beautiful and a little ironic.

poems.s: night moon river boat mist lantern
z: 烟笼寒水月笼沙，夜泊秦淮近酒家。
商女不知亡国恨，隔江犹唱后庭花。
e: Mist veils the cold water, moonlight veils the sand;
I moor on the Qinhuai at night, near taverns by the shore.
The singing girls don't know the grief of a fallen land —
Across the river they still sing "Rear Court Flowers", as before.
poems.n: The Qinhuai River in Nanjing was lined with pleasure houses. "Flowers of the Rear Courtyard" was composed by the Last Lord of Chen as his dynasty collapsed in 589 — the very sound of decadence and ruin. The real target is not the singers but the officials who request the song while the Tang itself declines.

poems.s: night autumn stars palace candle
z: 银烛秋光冷画屏，轻罗小扇扑流萤。
天阶夜色凉如水，卧看牵牛织女星。
e: A silver candle's autumn glow chills the painted screen;
With a little silk fan she chases fireflies as they fly.
On the palace steps the night is cool as water's sheen;
She lies and gazes at the Herdboy and the Weaver in the sky.
poems.n: A lonely palace lady on an autumn night. The silk fan was a symbol of a discarded woman, put away when summer ends; fireflies were said to breed in neglected grass. She watches the two star-lovers who meet once a year — more than she can hope for.

poems.s: day river wind sail fort
z: 折戟沉沙铁未销，自将磨洗认前朝。
东风不与周郎便，铜雀春深锁二乔。
e: A broken halberd in the sand — its iron's not yet gone;
I wash and polish it, and know it from that bygone age.
Had the east wind not blown to help young Zhou Yu on,
The two Qiao sisters, deep in spring, would be locked in Bronze Sparrow's cage.
poems.n: At the Battle of Red Cliff (208), Zhou Yu of Wu, helped by a timely east wind, burned Cao Cao's fleet. Du Mu's mischievous what-if: without that wind, Cao Cao would have won — and carried off Zhou Yu's wife and her sister, the famous beauties Da Qiao and Xiao Qiao, to his Bronze Sparrow Terrace. History turned on a gust of wind.

poems.s: dusk river pavilion boat
z: 胜败兵家事不期，包羞忍耻是男儿。
江东子弟多才俊，卷土重来未可知。
e: In war, no one can know beforehand who will win or lose;
To bear the shame and swallow pride — that is what makes a man.
East of the River there were many youths of talent —
Who knows? He might have rolled the dust back up, and come again.
poems.n: At Wujiang the defeated Xiang Yu refused a ferryman's offer to carry him back east of the Yangtze to raise a new army — he could not face the elders whose sons had died for him — and cut his own throat. Du Mu argues he should have endured the shame and tried again. 卷土重来, "rolling the dust back up", became the idiom for a comeback.

poems.s: day palace mountains rider horse
z: 长安回望绣成堆，山顶千门次第开。
一骑红尘妃子笑，无人知是荔枝来。
e: Looking back from Chang'an: hills like heaps of embroidery;
On the summit, a thousand palace gates swing open, one by one.
A horseman in red dust — the Consort smiles with glee;
No one knows it's lychees he has brought, at a run.
poems.n: Huaqing Palace on Mount Li was the winter retreat of Emperor Xuanzong and Consort Yang. She loved fresh lychees, so relays of horsemen galloped them a thousand miles from the far south, killing horses on the way, so they would arrive fresh. A whole empire's waste, in one smile.

poems.te: To Judge Han Chuo in Yangzhou
poems.s: night autumn moon bridge river hills
z: 青山隐隐水迢迢，秋尽江南草未凋。
二十四桥明月夜，玉人何处教吹箫？
e: Green hills grow dim; the waters stretch away;
Autumn ends, yet the southern grass is green.
On a moonlit night at the Twenty-four Bridges, say,
Where are you teaching a jade beauty the flute, unseen?
poems.n: Written to an old friend in Yangzhou, where Du Mu had spent happy, dissolute years. The Twenty-four Bridges of Yangzhou became a byword for romantic nights. "Jade person" can mean a lovely courtesan — or the handsome friend himself, teased about his pleasures.

poems.s: night tower lantern river boat
z: 落魄江湖载酒行，楚腰纤细掌中轻。
十年一觉扬州梦，赢得青楼薄幸名。
e: Down on my luck, I roamed the lakes and rivers, wine in hand,
With slender Chu-waisted girls light enough to dance on a palm.
Ten years — then I woke from my Yangzhou dream, to understand
All I'd won was a heartless rake's name in the houses of charm.
poems.n: Du Mu looks back on his years as a young secretary in Yangzhou, notorious for his nights in the pleasure quarters. King Ling of Chu loved slender waists; the Han beauty Zhao Feiyan was said to be light enough to dance on a palm. The self-mockery is tinged with regret.

poems.s: spring willow tower flowers
z: 娉娉袅袅十三余，豆蔻梢头二月初。
春风十里扬州路，卷上珠帘总不如。
e: So graceful, slender, just past thirteen years —
A cardamom bud on the bough as early spring appears.
Along ten li of Yangzhou's road in spring's warm air,
Roll up every pearl curtain — no beauty there compares.
poems.n: Written for a young singing girl as Du Mu left Yangzhou in 835. 豆蔻年华, "cardamom years" — a phrase from this poem — still means a girl of thirteen or fourteen. Behind every pearl blind on Yangzhou's famous avenue there were beauties; none matched her.

poems.s: night candle window two cup
z: 多情却似总无情，唯觉樽前笑不成。
蜡烛有心还惜别，替人垂泪到天明。
e: So full of love, I seem to have no love at all;
Over our cups I only find I cannot smile.
The candle has a heart, and grieves to see us part —
It sheds its tears for us till dawn, all the while.
poems.n: Too much feeling makes the lovers seem cold and silent. The candle's "heart" is its wick (心 means both), and its "tears" the dripping wax — so the candle weeps for the lovers who cannot.

poems.s: dusk spring petals tower river birds
z: 繁华事散逐香尘，流水无情草自春。
日暮东风怨啼鸟，落花犹似坠楼人。
e: The glory is scattered, gone with the scented dust;
The heartless water flows; the grass grows green, as spring has its way.
At dusk, in the east wind, the crying birds complain;
The falling flowers look like her who fell from the tower that day.
poems.n: The Golden Valley Garden in Luoyang belonged to Shi Chong (249–300), the richest man of the Jin, famous for his extravagance. When a powerful rival demanded his beloved concubine Green Pearl, she threw herself from a tower rather than be taken. Five centuries later, Du Mu finds only grass, water and falling petals.

poems.te: Climbing Leyou Plain Before Leaving for Wuxing
poems.s: day hills clouds rider wall
z: 清时有味是无能，闲爱孤云静爱僧。
欲把一麾江海去，乐游原上望昭陵。
e: To savour life in peaceful times, you must be no use at all;
At leisure I love the lone cloud; in stillness, the monk's way.
Now, with a governor's banner, I'll go where the rivers call —
From Leyou Plain, toward the Zhao Tomb, I gaze today.
poems.n: 850: about to leave the capital to govern Wuxing (Huzhou), Du Mu climbs Leyou Plain and gazes toward the Zhao Tomb of Emperor Taizong, the great founder of the Tang golden age. The first line is ironic: in such "peaceful times", only the useless can enjoy themselves — and he is not wanted. The look toward Taizong's tomb is a silent longing for a ruler who valued talent.

poems.te: Quatrain on the Rear Pond at Qi'an
poems.s: summer rain lake lotus oriole flowers
z: 菱透浮萍绿锦池，夏莺千啭弄蔷薇。
尽日无人看微雨，鸳鸯相对浴红衣。
e: Water-chestnuts push through duckweed — the pond's green brocade;
Summer orioles trill a thousand songs and play among the rose.
All day, no one watches the fine rain drifting through the glade;
Mandarin ducks, face to face, bathe in their red-feathered clothes.
poems.n: Du Mu as governor of Huangzhou (Qi'an). A rainy summer garden with no one in it — except a pair of mandarin ducks, symbols of happy love, whose red feathers are their "red robes". The poet's loneliness is felt only by contrast.

poems.s: autumn day tower mountains maple
z: 楼倚霜树外，镜天无一毫。
南山与秋色，气势两相高。
e: The tower leans out beyond the frosted trees;
The mirror sky has not one speck of grey.
The Southern Hills and autumn's clear expanse
Both soar, and vie in grandeur, high as they may.
poems.n: A crystal-clear autumn day in Chang'an. From a tower, the sky is a spotless mirror, and the Zhongnan mountains and the autumn air itself seem to compete to be loftier.

poems.s: summer wind petals peach
z: 自是寻春去校迟，不须惆怅怨芳时。
狂风落尽深红色，绿叶成阴子满枝。
e: It's I who came too late in search of spring;
I shouldn't grieve, or blame the flowering days.
The wild wind's blown away the crimson blossoming;
Green leaves make shade; the boughs bear fruit in sprays.
poems.n: Legend says the young Du Mu, in Huzhou, saw a lovely girl of about ten and promised her mother he would return to marry her within ten years. He came back fourteen years later to find her married, with children. Without the story, it is simply a gentle poem about missed chances — and about a different fulfilment: the fruit that follows the flowers.

poems.s: dusk desert river grass fort
z: 誓扫匈奴不顾身，五千貂锦丧胡尘。
可怜无定河边骨，犹是春闺梦里人。
e: They swore to sweep the Xiongnu out, with no thought for their life;
Five thousand men in sable and brocade fell in the northern dust.
Alas — the bones along the Wuding River, white and bare,
Are still the living men in the spring dreams of each wife.
poems.n: The most heartbreaking war poem in Chinese: the wives at home, not yet knowing, still dream of their husbands — who are already bones by the Wuding River ("River of No Fixed Course") on the northern frontier. "Sable and brocade" was the uniform of elite Han troops.

poems.s: night moon sea butterfly mist
z: 锦瑟无端五十弦，一弦一柱思华年。
庄生晓梦迷蝴蝶，望帝春心托杜鹃。
沧海月明珠有泪，蓝田日暖玉生烟。
此情可待成追忆？只是当时已惘然。
e: The patterned zither, for no reason, has fifty strings;
Each string, each bridge, brings back the years of bloom.
Zhuangzi at dawn dreamed he was a butterfly, lost in its wings;
Emperor Wang left his spring heart to the cuckoo's gloom.
On the blue sea, under the moon, the pearls are tears;
At Lantian, in the warm sun, the jade gives off a haze.
Must such a feeling wait for memory, across the years?
Even then, as it was happening, I was lost in a daze.
poems.n: Perhaps the most debated poem in Chinese — a love poem, an elegy for his wife, a lament for his career, or a poem about poetry itself. The legendary fifty-stringed zither was so sad that the god Fuxi split it into twenty-five. Zhuangzi dreamed he was a butterfly and woke unsure which was the dreamer; Emperor Wang of Shu became a cuckoo that cried till it bled; mermaids wept pearls; the jade buried at Lantian gave off a glow like smoke in the sun. Every image is lovely and out of reach — like the past.

poems.s: night spring candle window petals crescent
z: 相见时难别亦难，东风无力百花残。
春蚕到死丝方尽，蜡炬成灰泪始干。
晓镜但愁云鬓改，夜吟应觉月光寒。
蓬山此去无多路，青鸟殷勤为探看。
e: It's hard for us to meet, and just as hard to part;
The east wind has no strength; a hundred flowers fall.
The spring silkworm spins its silk until it dies;
The candle weeps till it is ash, its tears dried after all.
At dawn, before her mirror, she grieves her hair turning grey;
Chanting at night, she must feel the moonlight's cold.
From here to Penglai Mountain is not so far a way —
Bluebird, go faithfully, and see her for me, as of old.
poems.n: The most famous of Li Shangyin's "Untitled" poems. The silkworm and the candle are the supreme images of devotion until death — and 丝 "silk" puns on 思 "longing". The bluebird was the messenger of the Queen Mother of the West, and Penglai is the island of immortals: the beloved is as unreachable as a goddess. Teachers today quote the couplet to honour selfless dedication.

poems.s: night stars tower candle cup
z: 昨夜星辰昨夜风，画楼西畔桂堂东。
身无彩凤双飞翼，心有灵犀一点通。
隔座送钩春酒暖，分曹射覆蜡灯红。
嗟余听鼓应官去，走马兰台类转蓬。
e: Last night's stars, and last night's breeze,
West of the painted tower, east of the cassia hall.
Though I lack the bright phoenix's wings to fly to you with ease,
Our hearts, like the magic horn, are linked through all.
Across the tables we passed the hook; the spring wine glowed warm;
In teams we guessed at hidden things, by candles burning red.
Alas — the drums call me to my desk; I must away from you,
And ride to the Orchid Terrace, a tumbleweed blown ahead.
poems.n: A night of party games — passing a hidden hook, guessing concealed objects — where the poet exchanged glances with someone he could not openly approach. 心有灵犀一点通: the rhinoceros horn was believed to have a white thread running from end to end, so the phrase means two hearts that understand each other instantly. The Orchid Terrace was the imperial library, where Li Shangyin worked as a minor clerk.

poems.te: Written on a Rainy Night, to the North
poems.s: night autumn rain mountains window candle
z: 君问归期未有期，巴山夜雨涨秋池。
何当共剪西窗烛，却话巴山夜雨时。
e: You ask me when I'm coming home — I cannot say just when;
Tonight in the hills of Ba, the rain is filling autumn's pool.
When shall we trim the candle by the west window again,
And talk of tonight, when the rain fell on Ba, so cool?
poems.n: Written in Sichuan (Ba) around 851 to his wife — or a friend — in the north. The present lonely, rainy night is imagined as a future memory shared by candlelight, so the poem folds time back on itself; "Ba hills, night rain" appears twice, once in sorrow and once in comfort. "Trimming the candle at the west window" (西窗剪烛) now means a heart-to-heart talk with someone dear.

poems.s: dusk sun hills wall rider
z: 向晚意不适，驱车登古原。
夕阳无限好，只是近黄昏。
e: Toward evening, my heart was ill at ease;
I drove my carriage up the ancient height.
The setting sun is boundlessly lovely —
It's just that it's so close to night.
poems.n: Leyou Plain was the highest spot in Chang'an, with a view over the whole city. 夕阳无限好，只是近黄昏 — beauty at its height is already ending — is quoted of old age, of the late Tang dynasty itself, and of every last golden moment.

poems.s: night moon stars window candle palace
z: 云母屏风烛影深，长河渐落晓星沉。
嫦娥应悔偷灵药，碧海青天夜夜心。
e: Behind the mica screen, the candle's shadows grow;
The Milky Way sinks slowly, and the morning stars sink low.
Chang'e must regret she stole the elixir away:
Blue sea, blue sky — her lonely heart, night after night, till day.
poems.n: Chang'e stole the elixir of immortality from her husband, the archer Hou Yi, floated up to the moon, and lives there forever, alone. The sleepless speaker — a lonely woman, a Daoist nun, or the poet himself — understands her: immortality without companionship is an endless night.

poems.s: night palace candle two
z: 宣室求贤访逐臣，贾生才调更无伦。
可怜夜半虚前席，不问苍生问鬼神。
e: Seeking worthies, the emperor summoned back the banished man;
Master Jia's brilliance was beyond compare.
At midnight, sadly, the emperor drew his mat close — in vain:
He asked not of the people, but of ghosts and gods up there.
poems.n: Jia Yi, the brilliant young statesman of the Han, had been exiled; Emperor Wen recalled him and talked with him late into the night in the Xuanshi Hall, leaning closer and closer on his mat — about ghosts and spirits. Li Shangyin uses the story to mock rulers who chased Daoist mysticism (several Tang emperors died of "immortality" elixirs) while neglecting their people.

poems.te: Untitled (Your Coming Was an Empty Word)
poems.s: night crescent tower candle window
z: 来是空言去绝踪，月斜楼上五更钟。
梦为远别啼难唤，书被催成墨未浓。
蜡照半笼金翡翠，麝熏微度绣芙蓉。
刘郎已恨蓬山远，更隔蓬山一万重。
e: Your coming was an empty word; you've gone without a trace;
The moon slants on the tower; the fifth-watch bell is tolled.
In dreams we parted far; I wept, and could not call or hold;
I rushed this letter — the ink's too pale, not thick nor bold.
The candlelight half-veils the gold kingfisher quilt;
The musk scent faintly drifts through the embroidered lotus' fold.
Young Liu already grieved that Penglai Mountain was so far —
And you're ten thousand mountains beyond Penglai, I'm told.
poems.n: In a Han legend, Liu Chen met two fairies in the Tiantai Mountains, stayed half a year, and returned to find seven generations had passed — he could never find them again. The lover is now even further than that fairyland. The candle half-lighting the kingfisher-embroidered quilt and the drifting musk are the traces of a night together.

poems.s: dusk palace willow crows river sail
z: 紫泉宫殿锁烟霞，欲取芜城作帝家。
玉玺不缘归日角，锦帆应是到天涯。
于今腐草无萤火，终古垂杨有暮鸦。
地下若逢陈后主，岂宜重问后庭花。
e: The halls of Purple Spring lay locked in mist and rosy haze;
He wanted to make Wucheng his imperial home.
Had the jade seal not gone to the man with the sun-horned brow,
His brocade sails would have reached the world's end, to roam.
Today, in the rotting grass, there are no fireflies;
Forever, on the drooping willows, evening crows remain.
If underground he meets the Last Lord of Chen,
How could he ask for "Flowers of the Rear Court" again?
poems.n: Emperor Yang of Sui (r. 604–618) left his capital for pleasure cruises to Yangzhou (Wucheng) in dragon boats with brocade sails, bankrupting the state; he was murdered, and the empire passed to Li Yuan, founder of the Tang, whose "sun-horned" forehead was a sign of a destined emperor. Yang had fireflies gathered by the bushel to light his night outings, and planted the willows along the Grand Canal. The Last Lord of Chen lost his kingdom — to the Sui — while composing the song "Flowers of the Rear Courtyard". The two decadent rulers would have much to discuss in the underworld.

poems.s: summer dusk willow cottage
z: 本以高难饱，徒劳恨费声。
五更疏欲断，一树碧无情。
薄宦梗犹泛，故园芜已平。
烦君最相警，我亦举家清。
e: Living up high, you can hardly eat your fill;
In vain you cry, resenting the voice you spend.
By the fifth watch your cries grow faint, near still;
The whole green tree is heartless to the end.
A petty official, I drift like a broken spray;
My home garden's overgrown with weeds by now.
I thank you for your stern warning, cicada — I'd say
My whole household is as pure and poor as you, I vow.
poems.n: The cicada, believed to live on dew alone, was a symbol of the incorruptible scholar. Li Shangyin, trapped in minor posts by court factions, sees himself in the insect that sings itself hoarse on a tree that does not care.

poems.s: dusk spring petals pavilion sun
z: 高阁客竟去，小园花乱飞。
参差连曲陌，迢递送斜晖。
肠断未忍扫，眼穿仍欲归。
芳心向春尽，所得是沾衣。
e: The guests have left the high pavilion at last;
In the little garden, petals whirl and fly.
In tangled drifts they line the winding paths;
Far off, they see the slanting sun go by.
Heartbroken, I can't bring myself to sweep;
I gaze till my eyes ache, and long for their return.
Their fragrant hearts have spent themselves on spring —
And all they get is tears that wet my clothes in turn.
poems.n: Written around 846, when Li Shangyin was idle at home after his mother's death, his career stalled. The petals that give their "fragrant heart" to spring and receive only tears in return are his own devotion, unrewarded.

poems.s: day tower wall willow river
z: 迢递高城百尺楼，绿杨枝外尽汀洲。
贾生年少虚垂涕，王粲春来更远游。
永忆江湖归白发，欲回天地入扁舟。
不知腐鼠成滋味，猜意鹓雏竟未休。
e: The high wall winds afar; the tower stands a hundred feet;
Beyond the green willow boughs, there's nothing but isles and shore.
Young Jia Yi shed tears for the state, in vain;
Wang Can in spring went wandering farther than before.
I've always dreamed of going home to rivers and lakes, white-haired —
But first to turn the world around, then sail off in a skiff, set free.
I never dreamed a rotting rat could be such a delicacy,
That they'd suspect the phoenix chick, and never let it be.
poems.n: 838: the young Li Shangyin, having failed a placement exam because of factional politics, climbs a tower at Anding. Jia Yi wept over the empire's troubles as a young man; Wang Can, an exile, wrote a famous poem from a tower. In *Zhuangzi*, an owl clutching a rotten rat screeched at a passing phoenix — which eats only bamboo seed — fearing it wanted the rat. His rivals are the owls; office is the rat.

poems.s: night autumn moon frost tower geese river
z: 初闻征雁已无蝉，百尺楼高水接天。
青女素娥俱耐冷，月中霜里斗婵娟。
e: When first I hear the migrating geese, the cicadas are gone;
From the hundred-foot tower, the water joins the sky.
The Frost Maid and the Moon Goddess both can bear the cold —
In moonlight and in frost they vie, to see whose grace is high.
poems.n: Qingnü (青女) was the goddess of frost; Sue (素娥) is Chang'e, the moon goddess. On a cold, clear autumn night, the white frost and the white moonlight become two goddesses competing in pure, cold beauty.

poems.t: 宿骆氏亭寄怀崔雍崔衮
poems.te: Staying at the Luo Pavilion, Thinking of Cui Yong and Cui Gun
poems.s: autumn rain lotus lake pavilion bamboo
z: 竹坞无尘水槛清，相思迢递隔重城。
秋阴不散霜飞晚，留得枯荷听雨声。
e: The bamboo dock is free of dust, the railings by the water clear;
My longing reaches far to you, past city walls on walls.
The autumn clouds won't lift, and frost is late this year —
The withered lotus leaves are left to hear the rain that falls.
poems.n: Staying at a friend's pavilion, Li Shangyin thinks of two cousins far away. The last line — keep the withered lotus to listen to the rain — is among the most loved lines in Chinese: even dead lotus leaves have their beauty, as an instrument for the sound of rain. In *Dream of the Red Chamber*, Lin Daiyu says it is the one line of Li Shangyin's she likes.

poems.s: dawn spring palace window
z: 为有云屏无限娇，凤城寒尽怕春宵。
无端嫁得金龟婿，辜负香衾事早朝。
e: Behind the mica screen, with all her endless charm,
In Phoenix City, now the cold has gone, she fears the nights of spring:
For no good reason she married a man with a golden tortoise —
He leaves their fragrant quilt for the dawn court of the king.
poems.n: A young wife complains that her husband, a high official — the golden tortoise pouch was a badge of the third rank — leaves her bed before dawn for the morning audience. Light and witty, with a hint that ambition costs love.

poems.s: day palace lake horse clouds
z: 瑶池阿母绮窗开，黄竹歌声动地哀。
八骏日行三万里，穆王何事不重来？
e: At Jasper Pool the Queen Mother opens her latticed window wide;
The "Yellow Bamboo" song rings out, so sad it shakes the ground.
His eight steeds ran thirty thousand li a day, with pride —
So why has King Mu never come back round?
poems.n: King Mu of Zhou, in legend, drove his eight divine horses to the Jasper Pool in the far west to feast with the Queen Mother of the West, who offered immortality and asked him to return. He never did — he died. The poem mocks Tang emperors who sought elixirs of eternal life: even the fastest horses cannot outrun death.

poems.s: night stars palace horse flag
z: 海外徒闻更九州，他生未卜此生休。
空闻虎旅传宵柝，无复鸡人报晓筹。
此日六军同驻马，当时七夕笑牵牛。
如何四纪为天子，不及卢家有莫愁。
e: In vain they told of nine more continents across the sea —
The next life is uncertain; this one's done.
He hears the tiger guards beat out the watches, emptily;
No cockman calls the palace dawn — not one.
That day the Six Armies all reined in their horses there;
That Seventh Night, they'd laughed at the Herdboy's plight.
How could he, four decades the Son of Heaven, fare
Worse than the Lu clan, who kept Mochou home each night?
poems.n: Li Shangyin's sharp reply to the romance of *The Song of Everlasting Sorrow*. The tale that Consort Yang lives on in an immortals' island beyond the sea is empty talk. On the Seventh Night, when the Herdboy and the Weaver Girl meet just once a year, the imperial lovers pitied the stars — yet after nearly fifty years on the throne, Xuanzong could not protect his beloved as well as a commoner of the folk song, whose wife Mochou lived happily at home.

poems.s: night spring rain tower lantern geese
z: 怅卧新春白袷衣，白门寥落意多违。
红楼隔雨相望冷，珠箔飘灯独自归。
远路应悲春晼晚，残宵犹得梦依稀。
玉珰缄札何由达，万里云罗一雁飞。
e: Downcast, I lie in my white robe, the spring just new;
At the White Gate, all is bleak — nothing has come true.
Through the rain, the red tower looks cold, far off;
Past bead curtains and drifting lamps, I walk home alone, too.
On your long road, you must grieve as spring grows late;
In the night's last hours I still dream — faint, but of you.
How can the jade earring and sealed letter reach you? —
Ten thousand li of cloud-net, and one wild goose flying through.
poems.n: The poet returns to the red tower where he once met his love and finds her gone, far away. The "White Gate" is Nanjing, a stock place for lovers' meetings. A jade earring was a love-token; the lone goose, a letter-carrier, is lost in a net of clouds.

poems.s: dusk summer sun tower window birds grass
z: 深居俯夹城，春去夏犹清。
天意怜幽草，人间重晚晴。
并添高阁迥，微注小窗明。
越鸟巢干后，归飞体更轻。
e: Living secluded, I look down on the walled lane's way;
Spring has gone, but summer still is clear and bright.
Heaven pities the shy grass in the shade;
The world treasures the clearing at evening light.
It lengthens the view from the high pavilion;
It gently pours brightness through my small window's frame.
The southern birds' nests are dry at last —
Flying home, they're lighter than when they came.
poems.n: Guilin, 847, as a long rain clears at evening. 天意怜幽草，人间重晚晴 — "Heaven pities the hidden grass; the world treasures the late clearing" — is quoted for kindness to the overlooked and for the beauty of a good old age. Li Shangyin had just found a post after years of frustration; the light, dry birds are his relief.

poems.s: night spring flowers candle person
z: 寻芳不觉醉流霞，倚树沉眠日已斜。
客散酒醒深夜后，更持红烛赏残花。
e: Seeking flowers, I got drunk on rosy wine before I knew;
I leaned against a tree and slept; the sun had slanted low.
The guests gone, I woke sober, deep into the night —
And took a red candle out to see the last blooms glow.
poems.n: "Flowing Rosy Cloud" (流霞) was the wine of the immortals. Sober at midnight, the poet cannot bear to waste the flowers' last hours. Su Shi later borrowed the idea: "afraid the flowers will fall asleep in the night, I light a tall candle to shine on their red faces."

poems.s: dusk autumn mountains temple leaves clouds person
z: 残阳西入崦，茅屋访孤僧。
落叶人何在，寒云路几层。
独敲初夜磬，闲倚一枝藤。
世界微尘里，吾宁爱与憎。
e: The setting sun sinks behind the western peak;
I come to a thatched hut, a lone monk to seek.
Among the falling leaves — where can he be?
Through cold clouds, how many tiers of path to see?
Alone, he strikes the stone chime as night begins;
At ease, he leans upon a single staff of vine.
The whole wide world lies in a mote of dust —
Why should I love or hate? Why should I pine?
poems.n: A visit to a hermit monk on a mountain called Green Vine. The ending is pure Buddhism: if the whole universe can lie within a speck of dust, the poet's own loves and hatreds are as nothing.

poems.s: spring rain lotus lake palace wind
z: 飒飒东风细雨来，芙蓉塘外有轻雷。
金蟾啮锁烧香入，玉虎牵丝汲井回。
贾氏窥帘韩掾少，宓妃留枕魏王才。
春心莫共花争发，一寸相思一寸灰。
e: Soughing, the east wind comes with fine rain;
Beyond the lotus pond, a soft thunder rolls.
The gold-toad lock is fast — yet incense smoke slips in;
The jade-tiger winch draws silk rope, and water climbs the well.
Lady Jia peeked through the curtain, for young Han was fair;
Princess Fu gave her pillow to the Prince of Wei, for his flair.
O spring heart, don't race the flowers to burst into bloom:
For every inch of longing, an inch of ash lies there.
poems.n: Thunder, rain, lotus, a locked door, a well: hints of a secret love. Even a locked door lets in incense, and even a deep well yields its water — 丝 "silk" again punning on 思 "longing". Lady Jia glimpsed the handsome Han Shou through a screen and secretly married him; the goddess of the Luo River (Princess Fu) was said to have left a pillow for the poet Cao Zhi. The last line, "an inch of longing, an inch of ash", is the bitterest image of love's cost in Chinese — like incense that burns itself away.
